stem: Your app sends the same 20k-token system prompt on every request, followed by a short user message. What cuts cost **and** latency the most?

choices.text: Enable prompt caching on the system prompt
choices.reason: The repeated prefix is read from cache: cache reads cost a small fraction of the base input price (0.1× on most models, lower on some newer ones) and processing time drops.

choices.text: Stream the response
choices.reason: Streaming changes how output **arrives**; it doesn't discount the 20k input tokens processed on every request.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens`
choices.reason: `max_tokens` caps output length only; it has no effect on input cost or speed.

choices.text: Send requests through the Message Batches API
choices.reason: Batches are cheaper but asynchronous (most finish within an hour), so latency goes **up**, not down.

takeaway: A big prefix that repeats should be **cached**; streaming doesn't make input cheaper.
explanation: The key detail is that a large prefix is **identical on every request**, which is exactly what prompt caching is for: the repeated part is read from cache at a fraction of the input price and is processed faster. The stem asks for cost **and** latency, which rules out Option D: batches are cheaper but asynchronous, so latency goes up. Streaming (B) only changes how output arrives, and `max_tokens` (C) caps output length; neither touches the 20k input tokens.
mnemonic: Same start, every time? Cache it.

diagram.caption: Only the new part is processed at full price.

stem: Each request contains tool definitions, a long unchanging system prompt, then a block with the current timestamp and the user's message. Where should the `cache_control` breakpoint go?

choices.text: On the timestamp-and-message block, so the whole prompt is cached
choices.reason: That block changes every request, so the prefix never matches again; put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix, not on the varying block.

choices.text: On the last block of the system prompt
choices.reason: Correct: mark the last block whose prefix is identical across requests; the tools and system prompt before it are cached too.

choices.text: Move the timestamp to the very start of the prompt, then cache the rest
choices.reason: The cache is a prefix: a change early in the prompt invalidates everything after it, so nothing would ever hit.

choices.text: On the first tool definition only
choices.reason: At best this caches only the first tool (and it may fall below the minimum cacheable length); the long system prompt would still be processed at full price.

takeaway: Put static content **first** and the breakpoint on the **last identical block**; varying content goes after it.
explanation: The cache works on a **prefix**: everything up to the breakpoint must be identical across requests to hit. Here the tools and system prompt never change, but the timestamp block changes every time, so the breakpoint belongs on the last static block (B), which caches the tools along with it. Option A is the tempting trap: marking the whole prompt sounds like more caching, but the varying block means the prefix never matches. Moving the timestamp to the front (C) breaks every later match too.
mnemonic: Static first, breakpoint at the seam, changes after.

diagram.caption: Cache prefixes build in this order; a change invalidates that level and everything after it.

stem: An internal tool caches a large system prompt, but users often pause 20–40 minutes between requests, so almost every request pays for a new cache write. What helps?

choices.text: Nothing needed: cached prefixes stay valid for 24 hours after they're written
choices.reason: The default cache lifetime is **5 minutes**, which is why these requests keep missing.

choices.text: Add more cache breakpoints to cache each section separately
choices.reason: Up to 4 breakpoints let you cache sections separately; they don't make any entry live longer.

choices.text: Set `"ttl": "1h"` on `cache_control` to use the 1-hour cache duration
choices.reason: Correct: the 1-hour option exists for gaps longer than 5 minutes; its writes cost 2× base input instead of 1.25×.

choices.text: Trim the system prompt below the minimum cacheable length so it stops writing
choices.reason: A prompt shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length can't be cached at all, so you'd lose caching entirely.

takeaway: The cache lives **5 minutes** by default and is refreshed free on each hit; use `ttl: "1h"` when gaps are longer.
explanation: The clue is the **20–40 minute gap**: the default cache lives only 5 minutes, so each returning user arrives after the entry has expired and pays for a fresh write. Option C, `"ttl": "1h"`, is built for longer gaps, at the price of 2× base input on writes instead of 1.25×. Option A is the trap, since it assumes a 24-hour lifetime that doesn't exist. More breakpoints (B) split what's cached but don't make any entry live longer, and shrinking the prompt (D) just turns caching off.
mnemonic: Five minutes by default; an hour if you set `ttl`.

stem: An internal assistant now sends the whole 600k-token company wiki with every question, because the model has a 1M-token window. Answers have become less accurate. What best explains it?

choices.text: Accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows, so curate what's in the context
choices.reason: Correct: the docs call this context rot. More context isn't automatically better, so choosing what's in context is as important as the space available.

choices.text: The request exceeds the context window, so the API truncates the end of the wiki
choices.reason: 600k tokens is well inside a 1M-token window, so nothing has been cut off.

choices.text: Requests this long are billed at a long-context premium tier that lowers quality
choices.reason: Most 1M-window models bill long context at standard pricing (Claude Haiku 5.5 charges more over 100k tokens), and price doesn't change answer quality anyway.

choices.text: The API drops the oldest content first-in, first-out, so the system prompt is lost
choices.reason: That rolling behavior describes chat interfaces such as claude.ai; in API requests the content you send is preserved.

takeaway: A bigger window isn't a reason to fill it: accuracy and recall **degrade** as context grows (context rot).
explanation: The principle is **context rot**: accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows, so more context isn't automatically better. The 600k wiki fits easily inside the 1M window, which rules out truncation (B) and points to A: curate what goes into context. Option C is tempting because long prompts can sound like a pricing issue, but most 1M-window models bill long context at standard pricing, and price doesn't change answer quality anyway. Dropping content first-in, first-out (D) is chat-interface behavior, not the API.

stem: You cache a 300k-token document prefix on a 1M-token model. A teammate says the cache means those 300k tokens no longer take up context space, leaving room for 1M tokens of conversation. What's correct?

choices.text: Right: only uncached `input_tokens` count toward the context window limit
choices.reason: With caching, input is split across `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and all three count toward the window.

choices.text: Partly: cached tokens count only on the first request, when the cache is written
choices.reason: Cache writes and cache reads both count: `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` each count toward the window.

choices.text: Wrong: cached prefixes still occupy the window; caching only changes their price
choices.reason: Correct: the docs say cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window. Caching changes the price of those tokens, not whether they count.

choices.text: Right, but only for a prefix in the system prompt; cached messages still count fully
choices.reason: Everything in the request counts toward the window, the system prompt included, whether or not it is cached.

takeaway: Caching changes the **price** of prefix tokens, not the **space** they take in the context window.
explanation: Caching changes the **price** of prefix tokens, not the **space** they take: cached prefixes still occupy the context window, so C is right. With caching, input is split across `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and all three count toward the window. That rules out Option A, the tempting idea that only uncached tokens count, and Option B, since cache reads count just like writes. Where the prefix lives (D) doesn't matter either; everything in the request counts.

diagram.caption: Every part of the request counts toward the window, cached or not.

stem: A new teammate says: "Claude is just a next-word predictor, so it needs elaborate prompt tricks before it will follow instructions." Which answer reflects Anthropic's glossary?

choices.text: Pretraining on curated question-and-answer pairs is what teaches Claude to follow instructions
choices.reason: Pretraining uses a large **unlabeled** corpus, and pretrained models are not inherently good at answering questions or following instructions.

choices.text: Claude is a bare pretrained model, so fine-tune it through the Claude API before relying on it
choices.reason: Claude is not a bare language model: it is already fine-tuned to be a helpful assistant. The Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning.

choices.text: RLHF only adds factual knowledge; instruction-following comes from pretraining on its own
choices.reason: RLHF trains the model to behave consistently with human preferences, including following instructions more effectively.

choices.text: Pretraining teaches next-word prediction; fine-tuning and RLHF made it a helpful assistant
choices.reason: Correct: pretrained models often need deep prompting skill, so fine-tuning and RLHF refine them; Claude has been fine-tuned to be a helpful assistant.

takeaway: Pretraining teaches **next-word prediction**; fine-tuning and RLHF are what make Claude follow instructions as an assistant.
explanation: The glossary separates two stages. **Pretraining** on a large unlabeled corpus teaches next-word prediction, and such models aren't inherently good at following instructions; **fine-tuning and RLHF** refine them, and Claude has been fine-tuned to be a helpful assistant (D). That's why the teammate's premise is wrong. Option A is tempting but swaps the stages: pretraining doesn't use curated Q&A pairs. Option B fails because Claude isn't a bare model and the API doesn't offer fine-tuning, and C understates RLHF.

stem: A slogan generator keeps producing near-identical taglines, and the team wants more variety. Their older model still accepts temperature, and a teammate suggests lowering it. Based on how temperature works, what would that do?

choices.text: Make outputs more varied, because lower temperature explores rarer, more surprising word choices
choices.reason: This is backwards: exploring rare, uncommon or surprising word choices is what **higher** temperature encourages.

choices.text: Make outputs more conservative, sticking closely to the most probable phrasing and answers
choices.reason: Correct: lower temperatures give more conservative, deterministic outputs; higher temperatures give more creative and diverse ones, which is the opposite of what they need.

choices.text: Make the replies shorter and more concise, but leave how varied they are unchanged
choices.reason: Temperature controls the randomness of the model's predictions, not how long the output is.

choices.text: Nothing noticeable, because temperature only changes the output of fiction prompts
choices.reason: Temperature controls the randomness of predictions in text generation generally; for fiction, higher temperature can vary the answers as well as the phrasing.

takeaway: Temperature controls **randomness**: lower means conservative and probable, higher means more diverse.
explanation: Temperature controls **randomness**: lower values give conservative, probable outputs, higher values give more creative and diverse ones. The team wants **more variety**, so lowering temperature (B) would push the slogans toward the most probable phrasing, the opposite of the goal. Option A is the trap because it reverses the direction: exploring rare, surprising word choices is what higher temperature does. Temperature doesn't control length (C), and it isn't limited to fiction prompts (D).

stem: On an older model that accepts temperature, a regression test sends the same prompt with temperature 0 and asserts the reply matches a saved string exactly. It fails now and then, though nothing in the prompt changed. What's the explanation?

choices.text: It's expected: even at temperature 0, identical inputs can give different outputs
choices.reason: Correct: the glossary says results are not fully deterministic even with temperature set to 0.

choices.text: Temperature 0 is fully deterministic, so something in the request itself must have changed
choices.reason: The glossary says the opposite: even with temperature 0, results will not be fully deterministic.

choices.text: Anthropic's API is non-deterministic, so run the test through a third-party cloud provider instead
choices.reason: The non-determinism applies both to Anthropic's first-party service and to inference through third-party cloud providers.

choices.text: Raise the temperature to 1 so that the outputs settle into one stable answer
choices.reason: Higher temperature leads to more creative and diverse outputs, so replies would vary **more**, not less.

takeaway: Don't rely on **identical** outputs: even at temperature 0, the API is not fully deterministic.
explanation: The rule from the glossary is that results are **not fully deterministic even at temperature 0**, so an exact-string assertion will occasionally fail with nothing changed (A). Option B is the tempting misconception, assuming temperature 0 guarantees identical output and hunting for a bug that isn't there. Moving to a third-party cloud provider (C) doesn't help, because the non-determinism applies there too. Raising temperature (D) makes replies vary more, not less.

stem: Your ticket-summary prompt includes four examples, all short billing tickets written in the same style. Now Claude summarizes every ticket, even outage reports, like a short billing note. What should you change?

choices.text: Remove the examples and describe the format in words only
choices.reason: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure; the problem is which examples you chose, not having them.

choices.text: Add many more billing examples so the pattern is clearer
choices.reason: More of the same reinforces the unintended pattern. The guide suggests 3–5 examples, and they should be diverse.

choices.text: Use diverse examples, including outages, each in `<example>` tags
choices.reason: Correct: examples should be relevant, diverse enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns, and structured in `<example>` tags.

choices.text: Merge the examples into the instructions without tags so they read as rules
choices.reason: The guide says to wrap examples in `<example>` tags so Claude can tell them apart from instructions.

takeaway: Few-shot examples should be **relevant**, **diverse** and **tagged**; similar examples teach unintended patterns.
explanation: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, but Claude also learns whatever the examples **share**. All four are short billing tickets, so outage reports get summarized like billing notes. The fix is relevant, **diverse** examples wrapped in `<example>` tags (C). Option B is the tempting trap: more billing examples only reinforce the unintended pattern. Dropping examples (A) throws away the strongest steering tool, and removing the tags (D) blurs examples with instructions.

stem: A team starting a new backend proposes a thin hand-written HTTP client for the Messages API instead of the official SDK for their language, arguing that a request is just one POST. What would they be taking on themselves?

choices.text: Nothing beyond typing the URL: streaming, retries and error handling behave the same either way
choices.reason: Each client SDK provides idiomatic interfaces, type safety, and built-in support for streaming, retries and error handling. A hand-written client has to supply all of that itself.

choices.text: The agent loop and tool execution, which the official SDK would otherwise run for them
choices.reason: A client SDK is a general-purpose Messages API client: you still send each request and handle each response. The agent loop comes from Claude Code, the Agent SDK or Managed Agents.

choices.text: Streaming, retries, error handling and typed interfaces, which the SDK otherwise provides built in
choices.reason: Correct: the overview describes each client SDK as a general-purpose Messages API client with idiomatic interfaces, type safety, and built-in support for streaming, retries and error handling.

choices.text: Shell scripting glue, since a backend without the SDK is expected to call the `ant` command-line tool
choices.reason: The `ant` CLI is for shell scripting and interactive use. The general-purpose way to call the Messages API from application code is a client SDK, not shelling out.

takeaway: Hand-rolled HTTP means hand-rolled **streaming, retries, error handling and types**; a client SDK ships them built in.
explanation: A single POST is easy; what the SDK removes is everything around it that a production client has to get right: streaming, retries for transient failures, error handling and typed interfaces. Choice b is the tempting overreach: the client SDK is still a per-request client, not an agent runtime, which is what Claude Code, the Agent SDK and Managed Agents provide. Choice d confuses the CLI, meant for shell scripting, with the client library a backend would use.

stem: Your service wraps every official-SDK call in its own retry loop for 5xx errors. Logs show a single failing request reaching the API several times more often than your loop should allow. What explains this?

choices.text: The SDK already retries transient failures itself; configure its retries instead of adding a second loop
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK retries transient failures such as connection errors, rate limits and 5xx errors with exponential backoff, so each of your tries can become several attempts. A client setting configures or disables this.

choices.text: The SDK never retries anything on its own, so the API must be replaying failed requests on the server side
choices.reason: The official SDK does retry automatically: connection errors, rate limits and 5xx server errors, with exponential backoff.

choices.text: The SDK retries only 400 errors, so the extra attempts must come from elsewhere in your stack
choices.reason: The SDK retries **transient** failures. A 400 means a problem with the request's format or content, which retrying wouldn't fix.

choices.text: The SDK retries immediately with no delay at all; shorten your own loop's delay to match it
choices.reason: The SDK retries with exponential backoff and honors the server's `retry-after` header when present.

takeaway: The SDK retries transient failures **on its own**: configure its retries rather than wrapping it in another loop.
explanation: Two retry layers multiply: your loop retries a call that the SDK has already retried internally with backoff, so one failing request hits the API many times (A). The fix is to decide which layer owns retries and configure the SDK's setting accordingly, rather than guessing. The SDK does retry on its own (B), it retries transient failures rather than 400s (C), and it backs off rather than hammering (D).
mnemonic: Check what the SDK retries before you wrap it.

stem: While streaming a tool call, your code runs `JSON.parse` on every `input_json_delta` it receives and keeps getting parse errors. What should it do instead?

choices.text: Read the complete tool input from the `message_start` event, which arrives before the deltas
choices.reason: `message_start` carries a `Message` whose `content` is empty; the tool input arrives later, in deltas.

choices.text: Treat the tool input as a plain string throughout, since a string is the final type of `input`
choices.reason: The deltas are strings, but the final `tool_use.input` is always an **object**.

choices.text: Wait for a later `text_delta` event, which carries the finished tool input as one JSON object
choices.reason: `text_delta` updates text blocks. A `tool_use` block's input only arrives as `input_json_delta` partial JSON.

choices.text: Accumulate the partial JSON strings and parse once at `content_block_stop`, or use SDK helpers
choices.reason: Correct: the deltas are partial JSON strings. Accumulate them and parse once the `content_block_stop` event arrives, or let the SDKs do it for you.

takeaway: `input_json_delta` carries **partial** JSON: accumulate it and parse it at `content_block_stop`.
explanation: `input_json_delta` events carry **partial** JSON strings, so parsing each fragment on its own is guaranteed to fail. Accumulate them and parse once at `content_block_stop`, or let the SDK helpers do it (D). Option B is the tempting misread: the deltas are strings, but the final `tool_use.input` is always an object. Option A fails because `message_start` has empty `content`, and C fails because `text_delta` only updates text blocks; tool input arrives only as `input_json_delta`.

stem: Your Python chat backend streams replies through a hand-written SSE parser. It keeps breaking on events it didn't plan for, such as `ping` events and newly added event types. The official Python SDK is available to you. What does the streaming guide recommend?

choices.text: Keep the parser and freeze its event list, since event types are fixed for an API version
choices.reason: Under the versioning policy, new event types may be added, so a frozen list keeps breaking; code should handle unknown types gracefully.

choices.text: Move the stream to WebSockets, which carry one fixed message format
choices.reason: Messages API streaming is delivered as server-sent events (SSE); the guide offers no WebSocket transport to switch to.

choices.text: Stream through the SDK; handle raw events yourself only in a direct API integration
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says to use the client SDKs when streaming; only if you build a direct API integration do you handle the events yourself.

choices.text: Turn streaming off and show each reply only once it is complete
choices.reason: That gives up the incremental reply a chat needs; the guide's answer is to let the SDK handle the stream.

takeaway: Where an official SDK exists, **let it handle the stream**; raw event handling is the cost of a direct API integration.
explanation: The streaming guide recommends the client SDKs for streaming and says only a direct API integration has to handle the events itself (C). A hand-written parser takes on every detail of the event stream, including `ping` events and the new event types that may be added under the versioning policy. Option A is the tempting quick fix, but freezing the list means the next new type breaks it again. B swaps in a transport the API doesn't use, and D throws away streaming to dodge a parser bug.

stem: Your report generator runs on a network that drops long-lived connections at random. Each report uses a large `max_tokens`, and nobody reads the reports until the next morning. Which approach does the errors page suggest for coping with the unreliable network?

choices.text: Submit the reports as a Message Batch and poll for the results later
choices.reason: Correct: the Message Batches API lets you poll for results rather than requiring an uninterrupted network connection.

choices.text: Stream each report instead, since a stream needs no lasting connection
choices.reason: A stream arrives over a connection that has to stay up; batches let you poll for results instead of depending on it.

choices.text: Keep non-streaming calls and raise the client timeout a lot
choices.reason: Some networks drop idle connections however long the client waits, so the page warns against large `max_tokens` without streaming or batches.

choices.text: Cut `max_tokens` well below the reports' length so calls end sooner
choices.reason: That truncates the reports. The page's answer for long requests is streaming or the Message Batches API, not shorter output.

takeaway: When the network is unreliable and nobody is waiting, **batch and poll**: the results don't depend on one connection staying up.
explanation: For long requests the errors page suggests streaming or the Message Batches API, and it singles out batches for unreliable networks: you poll for results rather than needing an uninterrupted connection (A). Nobody needs the reports until morning, so batching costs nothing in speed. B is the tempting choice because streaming is the usual fix for long outputs, but a stream still depends on its connection. C ignores that networks drop idle connections, and D just shortens the reports.

stem: Your app base64-encodes a large stack of scanned PDFs into a single Messages API request, and the API responds with `413 request_too_large`. What does the error mean?

choices.text: The prompt has more tokens than the model's context window allows in a single request
choices.reason: A 413 `request_too_large` is about the request's byte size against the endpoint's limit, not its token count.

choices.text: The request body is bigger than the Messages endpoint's maximum request size
choices.reason: Correct: Messages requests have a maximum size (32 MB), and exceeding it returns a 413 `request_too_large` error.

choices.text: Your organization hit its tokens-per-minute rate limit on the Messages endpoint
choices.reason: Rate limits cap requests and tokens per minute and return 429; a 413 is the request-size error.

choices.text: The API key lacks permission to send PDF documents in a request
choices.reason: A permission problem is a different error; 413 `request_too_large` means the request is too big.

takeaway: A 413 `request_too_large` means the request's **byte size** is over the endpoint's limit, not that it has too many tokens.
explanation: A 413 `request_too_large` is about the request's **byte size**: the Messages endpoint has a maximum request size, and a body full of base64 PDFs went over it (B). A is the common confusion with the context window, which is a token limit with a different error. Rate limits (C) return 429, and permissions (D) aren't the issue.

stem: Your streaming client checks the HTTP status and treats 200 as success. A response returns 200, but partway through the stream an error with type `overloaded_error` arrives. How should you interpret it?

choices.text: Your API key is invalid or was revoked partway through streaming the response
choices.reason: Key problems are `authentication_error` (HTTP 401), and the request was already accepted with a 200.

choices.text: Your organization hit its rate limit while the response was being streamed
choices.reason: Rate limits are `rate_limit_error` (HTTP 429). `overloaded_error` means the API itself is temporarily overloaded.

choices.text: It can be ignored: a 200 status means the response completed successfully
choices.reason: When streaming, an error can occur **after** the API returns 200, so the status alone doesn't mean the response finished.

choices.text: A mid-stream error after a 200: the API is temporarily overloaded
choices.reason: Correct: streamed errors can follow a 200 response, and `overloaded_error` (529) can happen when the API has high traffic across all users.

takeaway: When streaming, a 200 isn't the end of error handling: errors such as `overloaded_error` can arrive **mid-stream**.
explanation: When streaming, the 200 status arrives **before** the body is finished, so an error can still occur partway through. `overloaded_error` (529) means the API itself is temporarily overloaded under high traffic across all users, which is D. Option C is the trap: treating 200 as final success ignores that mid-stream errors exist. Options A and B mislabel the error type: key problems are `authentication_error` (401) and rate limits are `rate_limit_error` (429), each with its own name.

stem: Your research agent runs on Claude Opus 5.5. It runs for hours doing multistep deep research, and your evals at `max` effort still fall short. According to Anthropic's guide, what should you try next?

choices.text: Claude Haiku 5.5
choices.reason: Haiku 5.5 is for the lowest latency and price: real-time apps, high-volume processing and sub-agent tasks, not the highest capability.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5
choices.reason: Sonnet 5.5 is for speed and capability on everyday coding, agent and enterprise work, not for when Opus 5.5 at max effort falls short.

choices.text: Claude Fable 5.1
choices.reason: Correct: if evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work, the guide says to move to Claude Fable 5.1.

choices.text: Lower effort to `medium` on Claude Opus 5.5
choices.reason: Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost, so lowering it gives up capability, the opposite of what these evals need.

takeaway: Start most workloads on **Opus 5.5**; move to **Fable 5.1** when evals at the highest effort still fall short.
explanation: The guide's path is to start most workloads on Opus 5.5 and move up to **Claude Fable 5.1** when evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work, which matches this hours-long research agent (C). Option B is tempting because Sonnet 5.5 is capable, but it targets speed and capability on everyday work, not going beyond Opus. Haiku 5.5 (A) targets lowest latency and price, and lowering effort (D) gives up capability, the opposite of what's needed.

stem: A high-volume, simple classification subtask runs on Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort. Quality is fine, but it's slower and costlier than it needs to be. Which change fits the effort guidance?

choices.text: Send `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` to skip reasoning
choices.reason: On Claude Opus 5.5 adaptive thinking is always on; requests that set `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` return a 400 error at every effort level.

choices.text: Raise effort to `xhigh`
choices.reason: `xhigh` is for long-running agentic and coding tasks and spends **more** tokens, which is the wrong direction here.

choices.text: Set effort to `"adaptive"`
choices.reason: `adaptive` is a thinking mode, not an effort level; effort values are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`.

choices.text: Set `output_config.effort` to `low`
choices.reason: Correct: `low` is the most efficient level, for simpler tasks that need the best speed and lowest costs, such as subagents. It gives significant token savings with some capability reduction.

takeaway: Effort trades thoroughness for speed and cost on **one model**: use `low` for simple, speed-sensitive work.
explanation: Effort trades thoroughness for speed and cost **on one model**. Quality is fine but the task is simple, high-volume and too slow and costly, which is exactly what `output_config.effort: low` (D) is for: significant token savings with some capability reduction. Option A is the tempting shortcut, but on Opus 5.5 adaptive thinking is always on and `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` returns a 400. Raising to `xhigh` (B) spends more tokens, and `adaptive` (C) is a thinking mode, not an effort value.
mnemonic: Simple and fast? Turn effort down.

stem: A nightly job on Claude Sonnet 5.5 summarizes the day's support tickets, and nobody reads the summaries until morning. Which change cuts its cost the most?

choices.text: Turn on fast mode so the job finishes sooner
choices.reason: Fast mode tunes synchronous latency, which this overnight job doesn't need; the calls are still synchronous requests at full price.

choices.text: Send the requests through the Message Batches API
choices.reason: Correct: batches suit work with no need for immediate responses, and usage is charged at 50% of standard prices.

choices.text: Set `stream: true` so each summary starts arriving sooner
choices.reason: Streaming changes how a response is delivered, not its price, and nobody is waiting on these responses anyway.

choices.text: Split the job into small groups of synchronous calls in a loop
choices.reason: Grouping requests in your own code isn't a Message Batch; each call is still a synchronous request at standard price.

takeaway: Work that nobody waits on belongs in the **Message Batches API**, at half the standard price.
explanation: Nobody needs the summaries until morning, which is exactly the Message Batches API's use case, and batch usage costs 50% of standard prices (B). Fast mode (A) and streaming (C) are about speed for someone who is waiting, and grouping synchronous calls in a loop (D) is not batching.

stem: You're moving a pipeline from Claude Sonnet 4.5 to Claude Fable 5.1 and plan to reuse last quarter's token counts to budget costs and check context fit. What does the token counting guide advise?

choices.text: Reuse them: a prompt has the same token count on every model
choices.reason: Claude Fable 5.1 uses the tokenizer introduced with Claude Opus 4.7, and a prompt counts roughly 30% higher on it than on earlier models.

choices.text: Multiply the old counts by exactly 1.3
choices.reason: The increase is roughly 30%, but the exact increase depends on the content, so a fixed multiplier is only a guess.

choices.text: Avoid the token counting endpoint, because each call is billed as input tokens
choices.reason: Token counting is free to use; it is only subject to its own requests-per-minute rate limits.

choices.text: Recount the prompts with the token counting API, passing the new model's ID
choices.reason: Correct: the endpoint counts under the tokenizer of the `model` you pass, and the guide says not to reuse older models' counts for costs or context fit.

takeaway: Token counts depend on the **model's tokenizer**: recount with `count_tokens` for the model you're moving to.
explanation: Token counts depend on the **model's tokenizer**. Claude Fable 5.1 uses the tokenizer introduced with Claude Opus 4.7, where a prompt counts roughly 30% higher than on earlier models, so last quarter's Sonnet 4.5 counts are stale; recount with the token counting API for the new model ID (D). Option B is the tempting shortcut, but the increase varies with content, so a fixed 1.3× is only a guess. Reusing counts (A) ignores the tokenizer change, and token counting (C) is free to use.

stem: A web dashboard shows progress updates that your server pushes while a long Claude job runs. The browser never needs to send messages back on that channel. Which browser API fits best?

choices.text: A WebSocket, because only WebSockets let a server push data to the browser
choices.reason: Server-sent events also deliver data from server to client, over a persistent HTTP connection; WebSockets aren't the only way to push.

choices.text: Server-sent events through `EventSource`, a one-way stream from server to page
choices.reason: Correct: server-sent events are unidirectional, server to client, which makes `EventSource` an excellent choice when the client doesn't need to send data back.

choices.text: `EventSource`, with the page sending its replies back over that same connection
choices.reason: Unlike WebSockets, server-sent events are unidirectional: messages are delivered only from the server to the client.

choices.text: A new HTTP request every second that polls the server until the job has finished
choices.reason: An `EventSource` opens a persistent connection, and the server sends events over it as they happen, so the page doesn't keep asking.

takeaway: Server-to-client only? Use **server-sent events** (`EventSource`); WebSockets are for when the client must send messages too.
explanation: The deciding detail is that the browser **never needs to send messages back**. Server-sent events are unidirectional, server to client, over a persistent HTTP connection, so `EventSource` (B) fits. Option A is the tempting assumption that only WebSockets can push data to the browser; SSE pushes too. Option C misreads SSE as two-way, which it isn't. Polling every second (D) is unnecessary, because an `EventSource` keeps the connection open and the server sends events as they happen.

stem: Your browser-based voice assistant streams audio chunks to your server while the server streams Claude's replies back, all on one long-lived connection. It needs wide browser support today. Which browser API fits best?

choices.text: WebTransport, because it's the simplest option and has the widest browser support
choices.reason: WebTransport has features WebSockets lack, but it's more complex to use and its cross-browser support isn't as wide.

choices.text: `WebSocketStream`, the standard Promise-based interface that every engine supports
choices.reason: `WebSocketStream` handles backpressure, but it's non-standard and currently supported in only one rendering engine.

choices.text: The `WebSocket` interface, which opens a two-way session between browser and server
choices.reason: Correct: the WebSocket API opens a two-way interactive session, so you can send messages and receive responses without polling, with good browser and server support.

choices.text: Repeated HTTP requests from the browser that poll the server for each new reply chunk
choices.reason: With the WebSocket API you can send messages to a server and receive responses without having to poll the server for a reply.

takeaway: Both sides send on one connection? Use **WebSockets**; the `WebSocket` interface is the stable, widely supported choice.
explanation: Here **both sides send** on one long-lived connection: audio goes up while replies come down, and the stem also demands wide browser support today. The `WebSocket` interface (C) opens a two-way session with good browser and server support. Option B is tempting because `WebSocketStream` handles backpressure, but it's non-standard and supported in only one rendering engine. WebTransport (A) is more complex and less widely supported, and polling (D) is exactly what WebSockets let you avoid.

stem: Your Python service must back off when the Claude API rate-limits it, but alert at once when the network can't reach the API. Today it searches each exception's message text for "429". What's the SDK-native approach?

choices.text: Catch `anthropic.RateLimitError` and `anthropic.APIConnectionError` separately
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK raises a typed subclass of `APIError` for each case: `RateLimitError` for a 429 and `APIConnectionError` when the API can't be reached.

choices.text: Catch Python's base `Exception` and keep matching on the message text
choices.reason: The SDK raises typed exceptions so you can branch on the class, not on fragile message strings.

choices.text: Check each reply's `stop_reason` for a rate-limit value
choices.reason: A rate limit raises an error (a 429 becomes `RateLimitError`); there is no reply with a stop reason to check.

choices.text: Set `max_retries=0` so errors come back as plain HTTP responses
choices.reason: `max_retries` only configures automatic retries; failures are still raised as SDK exceptions.

takeaway: Branch on the SDK's **typed exceptions**, such as `RateLimitError` and `APIConnectionError`, not on message text.
explanation: An SDK wrapping a REST API maps failures to typed exceptions: a 429 raises `RateLimitError` and an unreachable API raises `APIConnectionError`, so catch each separately (A). String matching on a base exception (B) is fragile, a rate-limited call returns no reply to inspect (C), and turning off retries (D) doesn't change how errors are raised.

stem: Your Python web service is built on `asyncio` and handles many user requests at once, each of which calls Claude. Which way of calling the API fits this code best?

choices.text: The sync `Anthropic` client with `stream=True`, which makes its calls non-blocking
choices.reason: Streaming delivers a response as events; for async code the SDK provides `AsyncAnthropic`, which streams through the same interface.

choices.text: A hand-written HTTP client, since the official SDK supports only synchronous calls
choices.reason: The SDK supports both synchronous and asynchronous operation, so there's no need to hand-write one.

choices.text: The Message Batches API, which is how the SDK runs requests concurrently
choices.reason: Batch results are read only after the batch has been processed, which doesn't suit users waiting on a reply.

choices.text: `AsyncAnthropic`, awaiting each call; it has the same interface as the sync client
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK supports asynchronous use through `AsyncAnthropic`, whose calls you `await`, with the same interface as the synchronous client.

takeaway: For `async` code, use the SDK's **async client** (`AsyncAnthropic`) and `await` each call.
explanation: The SDK wraps the REST API for both sync and async code; an `asyncio` service should use `AsyncAnthropic` and await its calls (D). Streaming (A) changes how a response arrives, not whether the client is async. The SDK already supports async (B), and batches (C) return results only after processing ends, so they don't fit live user requests.

stem: Your team is replacing hand-written HTTP calls to the Claude API with an official client SDK. Which of these will the SDK take care of for you?

choices.text: Raising your organization's rate limits after repeated 429 errors
choices.reason: Limits are set by usage tier; for higher limits you request a tier increase in the Console.

choices.text: Splitting oversized Messages requests so they avoid a 413 error
choices.reason: The maximum request size still applies; larger requests get a 413 `request_too_large` error.

choices.text: Sending the auth and version headers, and retrying failed requests
choices.reason: Correct: automatic header management (auth, `anthropic-version`, `content-type`) and built-in retry logic are listed SDK benefits.

choices.text: Picking the cheapest model that can handle each prompt
choices.reason: You choose the model in each request; the SDK sends what you ask for.

takeaway: SDKs handle the plumbing: **headers, retries, timeouts, types and streaming**. Limits and request size stay your job.
explanation: The SDKs take over the plumbing of each request: they send the auth, `anthropic-version` and `content-type` headers and retry failed requests (C). They can't raise your rate limits (A), which depend on your usage tier, or get around the maximum request size (B), and they don't choose a model for you (D).

stem: A Python service creates its Claude client with the API key pasted into the code as a string, and the file is committed to the repository. What does the Python SDK documentation suggest instead?

choices.text: Move the key into the system prompt so the model can authenticate calls
choices.reason: The key authenticates your client's API requests; it has no place in the prompt, and the client reads it from the environment.

choices.text: Put the key in `default_headers` in the code so it is sent on every call
choices.reason: That still stores the key in source; the client already reads it from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` by default.

choices.text: Base64-encode the key in the code so that it can't be read in the repo
choices.reason: Encoding isn't secrecy: the key is still in source control, which the `.env` approach avoids.

choices.text: Let the client read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, set from a `.env` file kept out of git
choices.reason: Correct: the client reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` by default, and the docs suggest a `.env` file (for example with python-dotenv) so the key isn't in source control.

takeaway: Keep API keys **out of code**: the SDK reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment.
explanation: The SDK picks up `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment by default, and the docs suggest a `.env` file so the key stays out of source control (D). A prompt is the wrong place for a credential (A), and both a header literal (B) and an encoded string (C) still commit the key to the repo.

stem: A cleanup script calls `client.messages.batches.list(limit=20)` and loops over the result's `.data`. Your account has hundreds of batches, but the script only ever sees 20. What's the simplest fix with the Python SDK?

choices.text: Read `last_id` from the first page, which holds the total number of batches
choices.reason: `last_id` is the cursor for fetching the next page, not a count of batches.

choices.text: Loop over the `list()` call itself; the SDK fetches more pages as needed
choices.reason: Correct: list methods are paginated, and iterating with `for` (or `async for`) automatically fetches more pages as needed.

choices.text: Call `has_next_page()` first, which loads every remaining item into `.data`
choices.reason: `.has_next_page()` only tells you whether another page exists; `.get_next_page()` fetches it.

choices.text: Switch to the async client, whose `list()` returns every page in one call
choices.reason: The async client paginates too; you iterate it with `async for`, which fetches more pages as needed.

takeaway: Iterate the list call itself: SDK **auto-pagination** fetches the following pages for you.
explanation: List methods are **paginated**: `.data` holds only the current page, so looping over it stops at 20. Iterating the `list()` call itself with `for` (or `async for`) makes the SDK fetch more pages as needed (B). Option C is the tempting near-miss, but `has_next_page()` only tells you whether another page exists; `get_next_page()` fetches it. `last_id` (A) is the next-page cursor, not a count, and the async client (D) paginates the same way.

stem: Your integration sends `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` and validates every response against a strict schema that rejects anything unexpected. Which two kinds of change can Anthropic still make under that same version?

choices.text: Adding new values to the output, such as extra fields in a response
choices.reason: Correct: within a version Anthropic may add values to the output, so a schema that rejects anything unexpected can break.

choices.text: Removing an existing input parameter that your requests still send
choices.reason: For a given version, Anthropic preserves existing input parameters.

choices.text: Renaming an existing output field that your response parser reads
choices.reason: For a given version, Anthropic preserves existing output parameters.

choices.text: Adding new variants to enum-like values, such as stream event types
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic may add new variants to enum-like output values, for example streaming event types.

choices.text: Making an existing optional input parameter required on every request
choices.reason: Within a version Anthropic preserves existing input parameters; the input change it may make is adding **optional** inputs.

takeaway: A version keeps existing parameters, but **outputs and enum values can grow**: parse responses tolerantly.
explanation: A version pins **existing** parameters, but outputs can still grow. Within `2023-06-01`, Anthropic may add new values to the output, such as extra fields (A), and new variants to enum-like values, such as stream event types (D); a strict schema that rejects anything unexpected can break on either. Option E is the most tempting wrong pick, but the input change allowed is adding **optional** inputs, not making existing ones required. Removing inputs (B) or renaming outputs (C) would break the version's guarantee.

stem: Integration tests must send the app's Claude calls to a local mock server, while production keeps calling the real API. Both run the same code, which builds its client with a bare `Anthropic()`. How should the test setup redirect the calls?

choices.text: Turn on the SDK's debug logging in tests, which routes requests through a local server
choices.reason: Debug logging turns on the SDK's log output through Python's `logging` module; it doesn't change where requests go.

choices.text: Put the mock server's address in the test environment's API key setting
choices.reason: The API key setting supplies the key the client sends, not the host it calls.

choices.text: Override a default request header in tests so that it carries the mock's address
choices.reason: Default headers change request headers, and the SDK warns that overriding them can cause undefined behavior; they don't change the URL.

choices.text: Set the client's base URL in the test environment's config; leave the code as it is
choices.reason: Correct: the client's `base_url` can come from the `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` environment variable, so the unchanged `Anthropic()` call targets the mock.

takeaway: Keep one codebase and let **each environment's config** say where the client sends requests.
explanation: The constraint is the same code in tests and production, so the difference has to live in each environment's configuration. The client's base URL can be read from the environment, so the test setup points it at the mock and the bare `Anthropic()` call follows (D). Option A is tempting because it sounds like a test setting, but logging doesn't change where requests go. The API key (B) isn't the host, and headers (C) don't change the URL.

stem: A production Python service intermittently misbehaves when calling Claude. You want to see the SDK's own log output, but you can't change the code, only how the service is started. What should you do?

choices.text: Point the client's base URL at a logging proxy that ships inside the SDK
choices.reason: The base URL only sets where requests go, and the SDK has no built-in logging proxy; its logging is switched on separately.

choices.text: Turn on the SDK's built-in logging with its environment variable at startup
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK logs through Python's standard `logging` module, and setting `ANTHROPIC_LOG` to `debug` or `info` turns it on.

choices.text: Set the client to make no retries, so the SDK prints each failure it would have retried
choices.reason: The retry setting configures or disables automatic retries; it isn't a logging switch, and changing it means editing code.

choices.text: Add a default header that asks the API to include debug details in every response
choices.reason: Default headers only set request headers, and the SDK warns that overriding them can cause undefined behavior; they don't enable logs.

takeaway: The SDK can be configured **from the environment**: turn on its built-in logs at startup without touching code.
explanation: The constraint is no code change, so the answer has to be something set from outside the program. The Python SDK logs through the standard `logging` module and turns that on from an environment variable (B). Option A is tempting because the base URL can also come from the environment, but it only changes where requests go. Retries (C) aren't logging and need code, and default headers (D) change requests, not logs.

stem: A coding assistant on Claude Opus 5.5 writes long files, and users watch the code stream in slowly. The team will pay more per token for faster output, but won't accept any drop in quality. Which option fits?

choices.text: Turn on fast mode: the same model with faster output, at premium pricing
choices.reason: Correct: fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration, so output tokens per second rise with no change to intelligence, at premium pricing.

choices.text: Switch to a smaller, faster model and accept some loss in quality
choices.reason: The team won't accept a quality drop. Fast mode gets the speed from the same model weights and behavior instead.

choices.text: Send the requests through the Batch API, which adds fast mode by default
choices.reason: Fast mode is not available with the Batch API, so this option doesn't exist.

choices.text: Turn off streaming so that each finished file arrives all at once
choices.reason: Streaming isn't what slows output. Fast mode is compatible with streaming, which is where its gain is most visible.

takeaway: Fast mode = **same model, faster output, premium price**: use it when speed is worth paying for.
explanation: The team wants faster output with **no quality loss** and will pay more. Fast mode runs the same model on a faster inference setup at premium pricing, so it fits (A). A smaller model (B) trades away the quality they want to keep. Fast mode isn't available with the Batch API (C), and turning off streaming (D) doesn't make generation any faster.

stem: A product manager hesitates to enable fast mode on Claude Opus 5.5 for a coding assistant, worried that answers will get worse in exchange for the extra speed. What is accurate?

choices.text: Quality drops a little, because fast mode runs a distilled copy of the model at lower effort
choices.reason: Fast mode keeps the same model weights and behavior; the docs say there is no change to intelligence or capabilities.

choices.text: Quality holds, and fast mode is billed at standard rates while it is in research preview
choices.reason: Fast mode is billed at premium pricing: $8 / $40 per MTok input / output on Claude Opus 5.5.

choices.text: Quality is unchanged: it's the same model on a faster inference setup, at a premium price
choices.reason: Correct: fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration, with no change to intelligence or capabilities, at premium pricing.

choices.text: Quality is unchanged, but fast mode only works on requests under 200k input tokens long
choices.reason: Fast mode pricing applies across the full context window, including requests over 200k input tokens.

takeaway: Fast mode is the **same model with faster output** at a premium price; intelligence and capabilities don't change.
explanation: Fast mode runs the **same model** with the same weights and behavior on a faster inference configuration, so there's no change to intelligence or capabilities; the trade-off is premium pricing (C). That addresses the manager's quality worry directly. Option B is the tempting near-miss: it gets quality right but says standard rates, when fast mode is billed at $8 / $40 per MTok on Opus 5.5. Option A invents a distilled model, and D is wrong because fast mode pricing applies across the full context window.

stem: An agent on Claude Sonnet 5.5 runs at `high` effort. On routine tickets it explains its plan, makes many separate tool calls and writes long summaries. The team wants fewer, terser tool calls without switching models. What should they change?

choices.text: Raise effort to `max`, so the model plans better and needs fewer tool calls overall
choices.reason: Higher effort tends to make more tool calls, explain the plan first and give detailed summaries: the opposite of what they want.

choices.text: Leave effort alone: it only scales thinking tokens, so tool behavior needs prompt changes
choices.reason: Effort affects all tokens in the response, including tool calls and function arguments, not just thinking.

choices.text: Set a separate effort value on each noisy tool definition and leave the other tools as is
choices.reason: Effort is set on the request with `output_config.effort` (or per message, in beta); it isn't a per-tool setting.

choices.text: Lower `output_config.effort`, since lower effort combines work into fewer, terser calls
choices.reason: Correct: lower effort levels tend to make fewer tool calls, combine operations, skip the preamble and use terse confirmations.

takeaway: Effort shapes **every** output token, tool calls included: lower it for fewer, terser calls.
explanation: Effort shapes **every** output token, including tool calls and their arguments, not just thinking. Lower effort tends to make fewer tool calls, combine operations, skip the preamble and use terse confirmations, which is exactly what the team wants, so lower `output_config.effort` (D). Option A is the tempting intuition that more effort means smarter, leaner work, but higher effort tends to explain more and make more calls. Effort isn't a per-tool setting (C), and B wrongly limits it to thinking.

stem: A team runs an autonomous refactoring agent on Claude Opus 5.5 for over an hour per task, with token budgets in the millions. Evals show quality gains above `high`, but they don't want unconstrained token spending. Which effort level fits?

choices.text: `xhigh`, the level meant for long-running agentic and coding tasks
choices.reason: Correct: `xhigh` gives extended capability for long-horizon work: long-running agentic and coding tasks (over 30 minutes) with budgets in the millions.

choices.text: `max`, the level that puts a cap on how many tokens get spent
choices.reason: `max` is the opposite: absolute maximum capability with **no** constraints on token spending.

choices.text: `medium`, Claude Opus 5.5's default, which is tuned for long tasks
choices.reason: `medium` is the default on Claude Opus 5.5, but it's a balanced level with moderate token savings, not the long-horizon one.

choices.text: `low`, because long agent tasks need the most token-efficient level
choices.reason: `low` is for simpler tasks that need the best speed and lowest costs, such as subagents, with some capability reduction.

takeaway: `xhigh` is for long-horizon agentic and coding work; `max` removes every constraint on token spending.
explanation: Effort levels map to workload shape. This agent runs **over an hour** with token budgets in the millions, and evals show gains above `high`, which is the long-horizon case `xhigh` is built for (A). The other constraint is not wanting unconstrained spending, which rules out Option B, the tempting pick: `max` is the level with **no** constraints on token spending, not a cap. `medium` (C) is the balanced default, and `low` (D) is for simple, cost-sensitive tasks.

stem: After moving a workload from manual extended thinking to Claude Opus 5.5, a developer notices that some simple requests come back with no `thinking` block at all, while harder ones still have one. What explains this?

choices.text: The thinking budget is too low; set `budget_tokens` to at least 1,024 on those requests
choices.reason: On Claude Opus 5.5, `thinking: {"type": "enabled"}` with `budget_tokens` returns a 400 error; adaptive thinking is the only mode.

choices.text: Adaptive thinking decides per request whether to think, and can skip it on simple ones
choices.reason: Correct: with adaptive thinking, when the model skips thinking for a simple request, no thinking block is produced, whatever `display` is set to.

choices.text: The default `display: "omitted"` setting strips thinking blocks out of simple responses
choices.reason: `omitted` still returns thinking blocks, just with an empty `thinking` field; it doesn't remove them.

choices.text: Thinking was switched off on those requests because effort was set above `high`
choices.reason: Thinking can't be turned off on Claude Opus 5.5 at any effort level; effort steers how often and how deeply Claude thinks.

takeaway: Adaptive thinking means Claude decides **whether** and **how much** to think; a missing block on an easy request is expected.
explanation: With **adaptive thinking**, the model decides per request whether and how much to think, and when it skips thinking on a simple request no thinking block is produced, whatever `display` says (B). That's why easy requests lack a block and hard ones keep it. Option C is tempting because it sounds like a display issue, but `omitted` still returns thinking blocks with an empty `thinking` field. Option A fails because `budget_tokens` with `enabled` returns a 400 on Opus 5.5, and thinking can't be switched off (D).

stem: A team runs two features on an older Claude model that still accepts temperature: a fiction generator that should produce varied stories, and an extraction job whose outputs they compare across runs. Which statements match Anthropic's glossary?

choices.text: Higher temperature can vary the fiction's answers as well as its phrasing
choices.reason: Correct: higher temperatures give more creative, diverse outputs, with variation in phrasing and, for fiction, in answers too.

choices.text: Lower temperature pushes the model to explore rare, surprising word choices
choices.reason: That describes higher temperature; lower temperature sticks to the most probable phrasing and answers.

choices.text: Setting temperature to 0 makes the extraction job fully deterministic
choices.reason: Even with temperature set to 0, results won't be fully deterministic; identical inputs may differ across API calls.

choices.text: Identical extraction inputs may produce different outputs across API calls
choices.reason: Correct: the glossary warns of non-determinism in APIs, even at temperature 0, on Anthropic's service and through third-party cloud providers.

choices.text: Running through a third-party cloud provider removes run-to-run variation
choices.reason: The non-determinism applies both to Anthropic's first-party inference and to inference through third-party cloud providers.

takeaway: Temperature tunes **diversity**, but even at 0 the API isn't fully deterministic, on any provider.
explanation: Two separate ideas are tested. Temperature tunes **diversity**: higher values vary phrasing and, for fiction, answers too (A). And the API is not fully deterministic: identical extraction inputs may produce different outputs across calls, even at temperature 0 (D). Option C is the most tempting wrong pick, since temperature 0 sounds like it should lock outputs down, but the glossary says it doesn't. Lower temperature doesn't explore rare words (B), and third-party providers are non-deterministic too (E).

stem: A request to Claude Opus 5.5, which has a 1M-token context window, carries a stack of documents totalling 1.2M input tokens before any output. What happens?

choices.text: The API accepts it, then stops with `stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded"`
choices.reason: That stop reason is for input that fits while input plus `max_tokens` exceeds the window. Here the input alone is over.

choices.text: The API drops the oldest content first-in, first-out until what remains fits the window
choices.reason: Rolling first-in, first-out handling is something chat interfaces like claude.ai can do; the API preserves the content you send.

choices.text: The API rejects it with a 400 `invalid_request_error` ("prompt is too long")
choices.reason: Correct: if the input alone exceeds the model's context window, the API returns a 400 "prompt is too long" error on every model.

choices.text: The API processes it and bills tokens past 1M at a long-context premium
choices.reason: Input alone over the window isn't processed at any price: the API returns a 400 error on every model.

takeaway: Input over the window gets a **400**; input that fits but overflows with `max_tokens` is accepted on Claude 4.5+ and may stop with `model_context_window_exceeded`.
explanation: Separate the two overflow cases. Here the input **alone**, 1.2M tokens, is larger than the 1M window, and that gets a 400 "prompt is too long" error on every model (C). Option A is the tempting trap: `model_context_window_exceeded` is for input that fits while input plus `max_tokens` goes over. The API preserves what you send rather than dropping old content (B), which is chat-interface behavior, and input over the window isn't processed at any price (D).

stem: An agent on Claude Sonnet 5.5 hits "prompt is too long" well before the team expected. Their context budget counted only the user and assistant messages. Which explanations are correct?

choices.text: Its tool definitions count toward the context window
choices.reason: Correct: everything in the request counts toward the window, including your tool definitions.

choices.text: The model's training data takes up part of the window
choices.reason: The context window is a working memory for the request; it's different from the corpus the model was trained on.

choices.text: The system prompt counts toward the context window
choices.reason: Correct: the system prompt is part of the request, and everything in the request counts toward the window.

choices.text: Cache reads are counted twice: as reads and as input
choices.reason: With caching, input is split across three usage fields (`input_tokens` and the two cache fields), and all three count; it isn't double-counted.

choices.text: The API rejects any input plus `max_tokens` over the window
choices.reason: On Claude 4.5 models and newer, input plus `max_tokens` over the window is accepted; generation may stop with `model_context_window_exceeded`.

takeaway: Budget the **whole request**: system prompt, messages, tool results and tool definitions all count, plus the output.
explanation: **Everything in the request** counts toward the context window, not just user and assistant messages. That includes tool definitions (A) and the system prompt (C), which a budget counting only messages would miss, so the limit arrives early. Option D is the most tempting wrong pick because cache fields look like extra accounting, but input is split across three usage fields that all count once; nothing is double-counted. Training data (B) isn't part of the window, which is the request's working memory.

stem: A math tutoring app on Claude Opus 5.5 (thinking always on) must solve problems with the school's own method. The prompt only describes the method in prose, and results are inconsistent. What does Anthropic's prompting guide suggest?

choices.text: Ask Claude to write out its reasoning in `<thinking>` tags inside the response
choices.reason: On Claude Opus 5.5, a prompt that asks the model to write out its reasoning, for example in `<thinking>` tags, may be declined; rely on thinking instead.

choices.text: Turn thinking off so that the examples in the prompt can take full effect
choices.reason: Thinking is always on for Claude Opus 5.5, and multishot examples work **with** thinking, not against it.

choices.text: Replace the prose with a hand-written step-by-step plan for every problem type
choices.reason: The guide prefers general instructions over prescriptive steps; Claude's reasoning frequently exceeds what a human would prescribe.

choices.text: Add worked examples, each one showing a problem, the method and the answer
choices.reason: Correct: multishot examples work with thinking. Worked examples shape how Claude approaches similar problems in its own thinking blocks.

takeaway: With thinking on, **worked examples** (problem, method, answer) steer how Claude reasons; don't ask it to print its reasoning.
explanation: Prose alone leaves the school's method open to interpretation. **Worked examples** showing problem, method and answer work with thinking: they shape how Claude approaches similar problems in its own thinking blocks (D). Option A is the tempting old habit, but on Opus 5.5 asking it to write out reasoning in `<thinking>` tags may be declined; rely on thinking instead. Thinking can't be turned off (B), and the guide prefers general instructions over a hand-written plan for every problem type (C).

stem: A zero-shot prompt (instructions only, no examples) asks Claude to turn meeting notes into action items, but the format and tone vary from run to run. What is the most reliable next step?

choices.text: Add a single example and tell Claude to copy its exact wording every time
choices.reason: The guide suggests 3–5 examples, diverse enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns; a single example to copy is neither.

choices.text: Add 3–5 relevant, diverse examples of the output, wrapped in `<example>` tags
choices.reason: Correct: examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure; the guide suggests 3–5 that are relevant, diverse and tagged.

choices.text: Restate the format as short ALL-CAPS rules without explaining the reasons
choices.reason: The guide says explaining why a behavior matters helps Claude deliver more targeted responses, because Claude generalizes from the explanation.

choices.text: Paste the examples into the meeting notes themselves so they read as part of the input
choices.reason: The guide says to wrap examples in `<example>` tags so Claude can distinguish them from instructions; mixed into the notes, they blur together.

takeaway: Going from zero-shot to **multishot** (3–5 relevant, diverse, tagged examples) is the most reliable way to steer format and tone.
explanation: The symptom is varying **format and tone**, and examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer exactly that. Going from zero-shot to multishot with 3–5 relevant, diverse examples in `<example>` tags is the fix (B). Option A is tempting because one example seems simpler, but a single example to copy is neither enough nor diverse. ALL-CAPS rules without reasons (C) throw away the explanation Claude generalizes from, and mixing examples into the notes (D) blurs them with the input.

stem: On multi-step math problems, a Claude Haiku 5.5 app answers less accurately with thinking turned off than with it on. Why does thinking tend to help on tasks like this?

choices.text: Thinking raises the sampling temperature, so more candidate answers are explored
choices.reason: Thinking isn't a sampling setting: it's Claude working through the problem in its own words, in `thinking` blocks, before it answers.

choices.text: Thinking gives the model a built-in calculator that it calls while answering
choices.reason: No tool is involved: thinking is generated text in which Claude restates the problem, tries approaches and checks its results.

choices.text: Claude gets to try approaches and check intermediate results before it answers
choices.reason: Correct: without thinking, the model answers in a single pass; with it, Claude restates the problem, tries approaches, checks intermediate results and drops dead ends.

choices.text: Thinking tokens are free, so the model can spend more on the answer at no cost
choices.reason: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, even when the thinking text isn't returned, and they count toward `max_tokens`.

takeaway: Thinking replaces single-pass answering with **scratch work and checking**, paid for as output tokens.
explanation: Without thinking, the model answers in a **single pass**. With it, Claude restates the problem, tries approaches, checks intermediate results and drops dead ends before answering, which is why multi-step math improves (C). Option A is tempting because exploring candidates sounds like sampling, but thinking isn't a temperature setting; it's generated text in `thinking` blocks. No calculator tool is involved (B), and thinking isn't free (D): it's billed as output and counts toward `max_tokens`.

stem: On Claude Opus 5.5, thinking blocks come back with an empty `thinking` field, yet `output_tokens` is far larger than the visible answer. A teammate suspects a billing error. What's going on?

choices.text: A billing error: hidden thinking isn't charged, so the extra output should be refunded
choices.reason: You're still charged for the full thinking tokens; omitting the thinking text reduces latency, not cost.

choices.text: Only a summary of the thinking is billed, which is why the count looks so large
choices.reason: You're charged for the full thinking tokens, not summary tokens, so the billed count won't match what you see.

choices.text: Setting `display: "summarized"` would take those thinking tokens off the bill
choices.reason: `display` changes what's returned, not what's billed: the block is billed the same either way.

choices.text: It's expected: thinking is billed as output tokens even when its text isn't returned
choices.reason: Correct: Opus 5.5 defaults to `display: "omitted"`, but the full thinking is still billed as output tokens. Omitting reduces latency, not cost.

takeaway: Hidden thinking is still **billed output**: budget for it even when you never see it.
explanation: Opus 5.5 defaults to `display: "omitted"`, so thinking blocks come back empty, but the **full thinking is still billed** as output tokens. That's why `output_tokens` dwarfs the visible answer (D); omitting reduces latency, not cost. Option C is the tempting fix, but `display` changes what's returned, not what's billed. It isn't a billing error (A), and you aren't billed only for a summary (B); you're charged for the full thinking tokens either way.

stem: A cost dashboard prices input as `usage.input_tokens` × the base input price. After the app adopts prompt caching, input costs look implausibly low. What is wrong with the calculation?

choices.text: Nothing: with caching, `input_tokens` already includes cached tokens at a discount
choices.reason: `input_tokens` holds only the tokens **after** the last cache breakpoint, not all the input you sent.

choices.text: It ignores both cache usage fields, which are billed at their own rates
choices.reason: Correct: total input = `cache_read_input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens` + `input_tokens`, and reads and writes each have their own price multiplier.

choices.text: Cached tokens are free, so the low figure is right and only output needs tracking
choices.reason: Cache reads cost 10% of base input on most models, and 5-minute cache writes cost 25% more than base input, so neither is free.

choices.text: It should read `output_tokens`, where cached input tokens are reported
choices.reason: Cached input is reported in `cache_read_input_tokens` (and writes in `cache_creation_input_tokens`), not in output tokens.

takeaway: With caching, `input_tokens` is only the **uncached tail**: total input = cache reads + cache writes + `input_tokens`.
explanation: With caching, input is split three ways: `input_tokens` holds only the tokens **after** the last cache breakpoint, while `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` hold the rest, each with its own price multiplier. The dashboard misses both cache fields, so costs look too low (B). Option A is the tempting assumption that `input_tokens` already includes cached input. Cached tokens aren't free (C): reads and writes are both billed. Cached input isn't in `output_tokens` (D).

diagram.caption: The docs' example: 100,050 input tokens in all, but `input_tokens` is only 50.

stem: Finance wants monthly API costs per workspace, in USD, that reconcile with Anthropic's billing. Today each app adds up the token counts from its own responses. What should the team use?

choices.text: Keep summing response `usage` in each app, then convert the totals at list prices
choices.reason: The Usage and Cost API exists so you don't rely solely on response token counting, and its cost data is meant for reconciling with Anthropic billing.

choices.text: The Usage API's token counts by workspace, priced by hand at list rates
choices.reason: The Usage API tracks token consumption; USD cost breakdowns that reconcile with Anthropic billing come from the Cost API.

choices.text: The Cost API, with USD costs grouped by workspace
choices.reason: Correct: the Cost API returns USD cost breakdowns that can be grouped by workspace, for reconciling with Anthropic billing. It needs Admin API credentials.

choices.text: A spreadsheet that multiplies each app's request count by an average request price
choices.reason: A rough estimate from request counts can't reconcile with billing; the Cost API returns actual USD costs.

takeaway: For billing-grade cost by workspace, use the **Cost API** with **Admin** credentials, not per-response token sums.
explanation: Finance needs **USD by workspace that reconciles with billing**, which is what the Cost API returns when grouped by workspace (C); it needs Admin API credentials. Pricing Usage API token counts by hand (B) is still an estimate, summing response `usage` (A) is what the Usage and Cost API exists to replace, and an average-price estimate (D) can't reconcile with billing.

stem: Your team is moving a workload from an older Claude model to a newer one and must confirm that its prompts still fit the context window and the cost budget. A teammate proposes reusing the token counts measured on the old model. What should you do?

choices.text: Reuse the old counts, since every Claude model splits the same text into the same tokens
choices.reason: Newer models use a newer tokenizer, so the same input text can produce more tokens; counts from an earlier model don't carry over.

choices.text: Count with `cache_control` blocks set, so cached tokens are left out of the total
choices.reason: Token counting gives an estimate without using caching logic; caching happens only during actual message creation.

choices.text: Recount the prompts with token counting, passing the model you plan to move to
choices.reason: Correct: the token counting endpoint counts under the tokenizer of the `model` you pass, so recount against the model you plan to use.

choices.text: Convert the old word counts with a fixed words-per-token ratio for all models
choices.reason: The guide doesn't give a fixed ratio; it says to count your prompts with the model you plan to use, because tokenizers differ.

takeaway: Token counts are **model-specific**: before a migration, recount your prompts with the token counting endpoint on the target model.
explanation: Token counts depend on the model's tokenizer, and newer models can turn the same text into more tokens. The stem's decision is whether old measurements carry over to a new model: they don't, so recount with the target model (C). Option A is the tempting shortcut, but it assumes tokenizers never change. B misunderstands token counting, which ignores caching, and D invents a fixed ratio.

stem: Your chat app resends the whole conversation on every turn and never trims it. One long conversation's history alone now exceeds the model's context window. What happens on the next request?

choices.text: The API quietly drops the oldest turns to make room for the new message
choices.reason: In API requests, previous turns are preserved completely. Rolling first-in, first-out handling is something chat interfaces such as claude.ai can do.

choices.text: The request fails with a 400 "prompt is too long" error
choices.reason: Correct: if the input alone exceeds the model's context window, the API returns a 400 `invalid_request_error` ("prompt is too long").

choices.text: The API summarizes the earlier turns for you so the request fits
choices.reason: The API keeps every turn you send as it is; trimming or summarizing history is the app's job.

choices.text: The request succeeds, and the extra tokens are simply billed at a higher rate
choices.reason: Input over the window isn't accepted at any price; the request is rejected before anything is generated.

takeaway: The API keeps every turn you send: when the history alone outgrows the window, the request fails with a **400**, so trim or summarize in your app.
explanation: The API is stateless and preserves every turn you send. When the input alone exceeds the context window, the request is rejected with a 400 "prompt is too long" error (B). Dropping old turns (A) is something chat interfaces like claude.ai can do, not the API, and nothing summarizes history for you (C) or bills its way around the limit (D). Managing the history is the app's job.
