explanation: The current lineup is a set of capability tiers: Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, with comparative latency running from slower to fastest and price falling in the same order. That's why running everything on the top tier has a real cost in latency and spend. Choice c is tempting because smaller models sound more limited, but every current model supports vision and tool use; the tiers differ in capability, speed and price.

stem: Your team is starting a new internal assistant for long-running knowledge work. There's no tight latency budget, no eval yet, and nobody is sure which model fits. Where does the models overview say to start?

choices.text: Claude Haiku, since the cheapest model is the safest default
choices.reason: Haiku is described for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction and routing. The overview's default when you're unsure is Opus.

choices.text: Claude Fable, since the most capable model is the safest default
choices.reason: The overview reserves Fable for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or for when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet, since a mid-tier model is the default for every workload
choices.reason: Sonnet is described as the best combination of speed and intelligence, but the overview's start when you're unsure is Opus for most workloads.

choices.text: Claude Opus, the overview's suggested start for most workloads
choices.reason: Correct: the overview says that if you're unsure which model to use, start with Opus for most workloads. It's built for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work.

takeaway: When you're unsure, start with **Opus** for most workloads; reach for Fable only when demanding work or your evals say Opus falls short.
explanation: The models overview gives a direct default for the unsure case: start with Opus for most workloads, and its description, long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, matches this assistant. Nothing in the stem points to a special case such as tight latency. Choice b is tempting because the top tier sounds safest, but the overview keeps Fable for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or for when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short.

stem: Your company is planning two Claude features: real-time autocomplete in a text editor, where every keystroke waits on the reply, and nuanced contract review, where accuracy outweighs cost. Which starting choices fit Anthropic's model-selection guide?

choices.text: Autocomplete: start on the most capable model, since fewer mistakes matter more than speed
choices.reason: The guide's efficiency-first start suits applications with tight latency requirements, and here every keystroke waits on the reply.

choices.text: Autocomplete: start efficiency-first on Claude Haiku, and upgrade only for specific gaps
choices.reason: Correct: efficiency-first suits applications with tight latency requirements, and you upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps.

choices.text: Contract review: start on the cheapest model, since a review can always be redone later
choices.reason: Capability-first is for tasks requiring nuanced understanding and applications where accuracy outweighs cost, which is this feature.

choices.text: Contract review: start capability-first on Claude Opus, then optimize down over time
choices.reason: Correct: capability-first suits tasks requiring nuanced understanding and applications where accuracy outweighs cost considerations.

choices.text: Both: run one shared model for every feature, so that there's a single default to maintain
choices.reason: The guide picks a starting point from each application's needs: efficiency-first and capability-first suit different kinds of work.

takeaway: Match the starting tier to the workload: **efficiency-first** for tight latency, **capability-first** where accuracy outweighs cost.
explanation: The guide offers two starting points and says which work each suits. Autocomplete has a tight latency requirement, which is the efficiency-first case: start on a fast model like Haiku and upgrade only for specific gaps. Contract review needs nuanced understanding and accuracy outweighs cost, which is the capability-first case on Opus. Choice a is tempting because autocomplete mistakes are visible, but the stem's deciding detail is that every keystroke waits on the reply.

stem: You moved a chat feature to the fastest model tier, but replies still feel slow. Each request carries a very long prompt, asks for long answers and runs at a high effort level. What does the models overview say about latency?

choices.text: Tier latency is relative; prompt length, output length and effort also drive it
choices.reason: Correct: comparative latency is relative to the current lineup, and actual latency depends on prompt length, output length and thinking effort.

choices.text: The tier fixes latency, so slow replies must point to a network problem
choices.reason: The overview says actual latency also depends on prompt length, output length and thinking effort, all of which are long or high here.

choices.text: Latency is the same across tiers; only price and capability differ
choices.reason: The overview labels comparative latency by tier, from slower (Fable) to fastest (Haiku).

choices.text: Only the context window size affects latency, so a smaller one would fix it
choices.reason: All current models share a 1M-token window. The overview names prompt length, output length and effort as what drives actual latency.

takeaway: A tier's latency label is relative; actual latency also depends on **prompt length**, **output length** and **effort**.
explanation: The overview's latency labels compare tiers with each other, and it adds that actual latency depends on prompt length, output length and thinking effort. The stem stacks all three: long prompts, long answers and high effort, so a faster tier alone can't make replies quick. Choice b is tempting because the fastest tier sounds like a guarantee, but the label is relative to the lineup, not a fixed response time.

stem: An overnight job reviews contracts for risky clauses. Nobody waits on it, and a missed clause costs far more than the tokens. A teammate wants Claude Haiku because it's the fastest tier. Which starting point fits Anthropic's model-selection guide?

choices.text: Haiku, since the fastest tier is the right choice whenever a job runs unattended
choices.reason: Efficiency-first suits tight latency requirements and cost-sensitive work. Nobody waits on this job, and accuracy matters most.

choices.text: Capability-first on Opus, since accuracy outweighs cost and speed barely matters
choices.reason: Correct: capability-first suits tasks requiring nuanced understanding and applications where accuracy outweighs cost considerations.

choices.text: Haiku, since efficiency-first is the only starting point the guide recommends
choices.reason: The guide offers two starting points; capability-first is for complex tasks where intelligence and advanced capabilities are paramount.

choices.text: Run it twice on Haiku and keep the longer answer, since two fast runs beat one careful one
choices.reason: For accuracy-first work the guide starts on a stronger model; it doesn't suggest repeating a fast one and picking by length.

takeaway: Speed matters when someone is waiting. For unattended work where **accuracy outweighs cost**, start **capability-first**.
explanation: The trade-off is capability against speed and cost, and which side wins depends on the workload. This job runs overnight, so latency barely matters, and a missed clause is expensive, which is the capability-first case. Choice a is tempting because Haiku is fast and cheap, but efficiency-first suits tight latency and cost-sensitive work, and neither describes this job.

stem: Your model-choice eval set is 40 hand-picked edge cases that tripped up an earlier prototype, scored on pass rate alone. Most real traffic is routine. Which change follows the measuring method in Anthropic's cost-and-intelligence guide?

choices.text: Add more edge cases until the set covers only the hardest requests the team can find
choices.reason: The guide says to pull tasks weighted like real traffic, and here most real traffic is routine.

choices.text: Pull tasks from production logs weighted like real traffic, and record cost per task
choices.reason: Correct: the method pulls a few tasks from production logs, weighted like real traffic, writes outcome checks for each and records cost per task beside the score.

choices.text: Replace the pass rate with each answer's length, since longer answers show more effort
choices.reason: The guide's checks are task outcomes, such as tests pass, ticket closed or row count correct, not answer length.

choices.text: Stop scoring and let the team vote on which model's answers feel better
choices.reason: The guide writes an outcome check for each task and records cost beside the score; a vote gives neither.

takeaway: Choose a model on tasks that look like **real traffic**, with outcome checks and **cost per task** recorded beside each score.
explanation: A model choice should reflect what the model will actually see. The guide's method pulls tasks from production logs weighted like real traffic, writes an outcome check for each, and records cost beside the score, so you can see whether a cheaper model holds up. Here the set holds only edge cases while most traffic is routine. Choice a is tempting because hard cases feel rigorous, but a set of only the hardest requests misstates both quality and cost on real traffic.

diagram.caption: Measure on your own workload before you pick a tier.

stem: Your team is building a scientific app that solves multistep math problems, and accuracy matters more than cost. Following the capability-first approach in Anthropic's model-selection guide, what's the right sequence?

choices.text: Build on Claude Haiku, and upgrade only after users report wrong answers in production
choices.reason: That's closer to efficiency-first, which suits cost-sensitive and latency-bound work. This app is one where accuracy outweighs cost.

choices.text: Build on Claude Fable, since capability-first means the top tier for every task
choices.reason: Capability-first starts on Opus. The guide moves to Fable only if evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short.

choices.text: Build on Claude Opus and stay there for good, since downgrading always lowers accuracy
choices.reason: The guide's later step is to consider lowering effort or downgrading models over time, once you've evaluated performance.

choices.text: Opus first, tune prompts, evaluate, then lower effort or downgrade as evals allow
choices.reason: Correct: implement with Opus, optimize prompts, evaluate, then consider increasing efficiency by lowering effort or downgrading models over time.

takeaway: Capability-first: start on **Opus** to set the quality bar, then use evals to see how far effort or the tier can come down.
explanation: Capability-first means starting from the strongest starting point for the task, which the guide names as Opus, then optimizing prompts, evaluating, and only then trying lower effort or a cheaper model. Scientific and mathematical applications are on its list for this approach. Choice b is tempting because capability-first sounds like "use the top tier", but the guide starts on Opus and moves to Fable only if evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short.

stem: You started efficiency-first, with a prototype on Claude Haiku. Testing shows it handles almost every case well but misses one specific kind of multi-step request. What does the guide's efficiency-first approach say?

choices.text: Move the whole app to the most capable model, since one gap shows Haiku isn't enough
choices.reason: Efficiency-first upgrades only for specific capability gaps, and the testing shows Haiku handles almost every case.

choices.text: Ship it as is, because efficiency-first means cost always outranks quality
choices.reason: The approach evaluates whether performance meets your requirements, then upgrades if necessary for specific gaps.

choices.text: Upgrade only where testing shows a need: for that one specific capability gap
choices.reason: Correct: the approach's last step is to "upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps".

choices.text: Stop testing, since efficiency-first assumes the cheapest model is always enough
choices.reason: Its steps are to test your use case thoroughly and evaluate the results; the guide says this start is often, not always, sufficient.

takeaway: Efficiency-first: start fast and cheap, test thoroughly, and upgrade **only** for the specific gaps the tests reveal.
explanation: Efficiency-first starts on a fast, low-cost model, tests the use case thoroughly, and upgrades only if necessary for specific capability gaps. The stem's deciding detail is that the gap is narrow: one kind of request, while almost everything else passes. Choice a is tempting because a failure feels like proof the model is too small, but moving everything up pays the higher price for the many cases Haiku already handles.

stem: Your document Q&A service handles mostly quick lookups. Users can also tick a "deep analysis" box, and those requests need far more reasoning. You want low cost on the common path without shortchanging the hard cases. Which design is the routing workflow?

choices.text: Default each request to a fast, low-cost model, and send ticked ones to a more capable model
choices.reason: Correct: routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up, such as easy questions to smaller, cost-efficient models and hard ones to more capable ones.

choices.text: Send every request to both models, and return whichever answer comes back longer
choices.reason: That runs both models on every request, so the common path is never cheap. Routing directs each input to one specialized follow-up task.

choices.text: Send every request to the most capable model, so that deep analysis is never shortchanged
choices.reason: That ignores the cost goal. The post's routing example sends easy, common questions to smaller, cost-efficient models.

choices.text: Let the fast model answer everything, and retry on a bigger one when users complain
choices.reason: Routing classifies the input first and then directs it. Here the signal, the ticked box, is known before any model runs.

takeaway: Routing = a default model for the common path plus an override to a bigger model when a task signal says the request is hard.
explanation: Routing classifies each input and sends it to the follow-up that suits it. Here the classification is simple: the ticked box is a signal known up front, so the common path stays on a fast, low-cost model and flagged requests go to a more capable one. Choice c is tempting because it guarantees quality, but it pays the top price for every quick lookup, which is exactly what the post's easy-to-small, hard-to-capable example avoids.

diagram.caption: A default path plus an override on a task signal.

stem: A team wants to route requests between a small and a large model. In testing, neither an LLM classifier nor a rules-based one can reliably tell their easy requests from hard ones; the categories blur together. What does Building effective agents say about this fit?

choices.text: Routing still fits, because the larger model will catch and fix any misrouted request
choices.reason: The post's condition is that classification can be handled accurately. Routing sends each input to one follow-up; it doesn't describe a second check.

choices.text: Routing works only with an LLM classifier, so the rules-based one was never an option
choices.reason: The post says classification can be handled by an LLM or a more traditional classification model or algorithm.

choices.text: Routing fits any workload that has two models, whatever its categories look like
choices.reason: The post limits it to complex tasks with distinct categories that are better handled separately.

choices.text: It fits poorly: routing needs distinct categories and classification that's accurate
choices.reason: Correct: routing works well where there are distinct categories better handled separately, and where classification can be handled accurately.

takeaway: Route only when categories are **distinct** and you can **classify accurately**; a router that can't tell inputs apart sends them the wrong way.
explanation: The post gives two conditions for routing: distinct categories that are better handled separately, and classification that can be done accurately, by an LLM or a traditional algorithm. This team fails the second condition, since neither classifier can separate easy from hard. Choice a is tempting because a stronger model feels like a safety net, but routing directs each input to one follow-up, which is why the post makes accurate classification a condition up front.

stem: Your long-horizon research agent runs on Claude Opus. Even after you raise its effort, your evals show it still falls short on the hardest tasks. What does the models overview suggest trying next?

choices.text: Claude Haiku, since faster turns let the agent make more attempts in the same time
choices.reason: Haiku is described for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction and routing, not demanding long-horizon work.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet, since it's described as the best combination of speed and intelligence
choices.reason: Sonnet balances speed and intelligence. The overview's step when Opus at higher effort still falls short is Fable.

choices.text: Claude Fable, the tier built for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work
choices.reason: Correct: use Fable for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when your evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short.

choices.text: Stay on Opus and lower its effort, since less thinking makes long tasks more reliable
choices.reason: The overview's step when Opus at higher effort still falls short is to move to Fable, not to lower effort.

takeaway: **Fable** is the step up from Opus: for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when evals on Opus at higher effort fall short.
explanation: The overview's default is Opus, with Fable as the step up when the work is demanding or when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short. The stem has both: a long-horizon agent, and evals that miss even after raising effort. Choice b is tempting because Sonnet is well balanced, but the overview's next step from a struggling Opus is Fable, not Sonnet.

stem: Your support-reply feature runs on Claude Sonnet, and your evals show it comfortably clears your quality bar. A teammate wants to move it to the most capable tier "just to be safe". What would that move mainly cost you?

choices.text: Nothing: the most capable tier is also the fastest, so replies would arrive sooner
choices.reason: The overview labels the most capable tier, Fable, slower; Sonnet is fast and Haiku the fastest.

choices.text: Tool use and vision, which the top tier gives up in exchange for deeper reasoning
choices.reason: All current models support text and image input, vision and tool use.

choices.text: Higher latency and price per token, for quality your evals show you don't need
choices.reason: Correct: comparative latency runs from slower (Fable) to fastest (Haiku), and price per token falls in the same order. Your evals already show Sonnet meets the bar.

choices.text: Context, since the most capable tier has a smaller context window than Sonnet
choices.reason: All current models share the same 1M-token context window.

takeaway: Moving up a tier buys capability at the cost of **latency** and **price**; when your evals already pass, that's spend without a gain.
explanation: Higher tiers are more capable but slower and pricier per token, so moving up is worth it only when the extra quality matters. The deciding detail is that evals already show Sonnet clears the bar. Choice b is tempting because a top model can sound specialised, but every current model supports vision and tool use; what changes between tiers is capability, speed and price.

stem: Your app has called the same model ID for months. This week you notice small, unexpected differences in its outputs, though your code and prompts haven't changed. According to Anthropic's Model IDs and versioning page, what's the most likely cause?

choices.text: A serving-infrastructure update, like new sampling logic, around the same weights
choices.reason: Correct: weights are fixed for an ID, but infrastructure such as the request router, safety classifiers and sampling logic can change. That's the most likely cause.

choices.text: Anthropic quietly retrained the weights behind that ID and kept the same model name
choices.reason: Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID. An updated version ships under a new ID.

choices.text: The ID is an evergreen pointer, and it now resolves to the newest model in its line
choices.reason: Dateless IDs are pinned snapshots, not evergreen pointers to the latest or best-performing version.

choices.text: The model's knowledge cutoff moved forward, so its answers now reflect newer data
choices.reason: The weights for a given ID are fixed, so what the model learned in training doesn't change under that ID.

takeaway: A pinned model ID keeps its weights for life; small behavior shifts on a stable ID most likely come from **serving-infrastructure** updates.
explanation: Pinning a model ID fixes the weights: Anthropic never updates an existing ID, and a new version ships under a new ID. The serving infrastructure around the model, such as the request router, safety classifiers and sampling logic, can still change, and the page names that as the most likely cause of small shifts. Choice c is tempting because dateless IDs look like moving aliases, but the page calls that a common misconception.

stem: Your support bot defaults every request to a fast, low-cost model and should send the hard ones to a more capable model. Which signals could reasonably trigger that override?

choices.text: A classifier, LLM or rules-based, that has tested as reliable at flagging complex requests
choices.reason: Correct: routing classifies an input and directs it to a follow-up, and the classification can be done by an LLM or a more traditional model or algorithm, as long as it's accurate.

choices.text: A random sample of one request in ten, so the capable model sees a share of traffic
choices.reason: A random pick says nothing about the request. Routing depends on classifying the input itself.

choices.text: A product flag that marks the request as hard, such as a user choosing "expert review"
choices.reason: Correct: a known flag is a simple, accurate classification of the input, so easy requests stay on the small model and flagged ones go to the capable one.

choices.text: The time of day, so the capable model handles every request during business hours
choices.reason: The clock doesn't describe the request. Routing sends hard or unusual questions to more capable models based on what the input is.

choices.text: The bot's overall error rate, so all traffic moves to the capable model when errors rise
choices.reason: That moves every request at once, whatever its difficulty. Routing classifies each input and directs it to the follow-up that suits it.

takeaway: An override needs a **task signal** about the request itself: an accurate classifier or an explicit flag, not chance or the clock.
explanation: Routing classifies each input and sends it to the model that suits it, so the trigger must say something about the request: a classifier that has proven accurate, or a flag that marks it as hard. Random sampling, the time of day and an overall error rate all ignore what the request is. Choice b is tempting because it does send some traffic to the capable model, but not the hard requests in particular.

stem: A newly released model looks promising for your production summarizer. You want to switch without surprising users. Which plan follows the method in Anthropic's cost-and-intelligence guide?

choices.text: Switch all traffic on release day, since a newer model does better on every prompt
choices.reason: The guide's numbers drift as models and prices change, which is why it says to measure on your own workload before cutover.

choices.text: Re-run your eval suite on the new model, shadow it on a traffic slice, then cut over
choices.reason: Correct: the method ends with "run the winner in shadow on a traffic slice before cutover, then keep the suite running."

choices.text: Change the model ID in production, then retire the eval suite once error rates look normal
choices.reason: The guide says to keep the suite running after cutover, and its checks are task outcomes, not error rates.

choices.text: Wait for a public leaderboard result, then switch if the new model ranks higher
choices.reason: The guide's method measures on your own workload, using tasks pulled from your production logs.

takeaway: Upgrade like any model change: re-run **your** evals, **shadow** on a traffic slice, cut over, and keep the suite running.
explanation: A new model is a new configuration to measure, not an automatic win. The guide's method runs the candidate on your own eval suite, then runs the winner in shadow on a slice of real traffic before cutover, and keeps the suite running afterwards. Choice a is tempting because newer models are often stronger overall, but the guide's whole method exists because results on your workload can differ from general expectations.

diagram.caption: Upgrade only after your own evals and a shadow run agree.

stem: Your Agent SDK agent is about to go to production. You want enough observability to explain afterwards why a run was slow or expensive. Per the SDK's observability guide, what do you need visibility into?

choices.text: Only the final answer of each run, stored in full so that reviewers can read every response later
choices.reason: The guide asks for structural, step-level data. Prompt and output content isn't even exported by default; durations, model names and tool names are.

choices.text: Which tools ran, how long each model request took, the tokens spent and where failures occurred
choices.reason: Correct: the guide lists exactly these: which tools were called, how long each model request took, how many tokens were spent and where failures occurred.

choices.text: Only the monthly invoice total, since per-request numbers are too noisy to act on in production
choices.reason: The guide wants per-request visibility, such as how long each model request took and how many tokens it spent, so you can find the slow or costly step.

choices.text: Only whether each run finished, since the outcome matters far more than the steps that led to it
choices.reason: A pass/fail outcome can't explain a slow or costly run; the guide asks for tool calls, request durations, tokens and failure points.

takeaway: Observability per call means **tokens**, **latency** and **errors** (plus which tools ran), so you can find the step that's slow or costly.
explanation: Cost and latency are invisible until you instrument them, so production agents need per-step data: tool calls, how long each model request took, tokens spent and where failures happened. The stem's goal, explaining a slow or expensive run after the fact, needs exactly that step-level view. Choice c is tempting because the invoice does show cost, but a monthly total can't tell you which call or step caused it.

stem: Your Agent SDK pipeline runs a lead agent on Opus that delegates to subagents on Haiku, and the monthly bill is over budget. The team wants to shorten every prompt across the board. What should they do first?

choices.text: Trim every prompt by the same share right away, since each step contributes to the bill equally
choices.reason: That cuts blindly. The SDK reports per-step usage and a per-model breakdown precisely so you can see where tokens are going before changing anything.

choices.text: Cut the lead agent's prompt first, since the lead model is always where most of the spend goes
choices.reason: That's a guess. A flow can look uniformly expensive while one step does most of the spending, so measure per step and per model before deciding what to cut.

choices.text: Break usage down per step and per model, find where the tokens go, then optimize that part
choices.reason: Correct: per-step usage and the per-model breakdown (`modelUsage`) show where tokens are going, for example the Haiku subagents versus the Opus lead.

choices.text: Move every step to the smallest model first, then check whether the bill went down
choices.reason: Changing models before measuring guesses at the cause; the per-model breakdown tells you which model's tokens actually make up the spend.

takeaway: **Measure before you optimize**: break spend down per step and per model, then put the effort where the tokens actually go.
explanation: A flow can look uniformly expensive while one step does most of the spending, so the first move is measurement, not cuts. The SDK's per-step usage and per-model breakdown show where the tokens go in a run that mixes a lead model and subagent models. Choice d is tempting because a smaller model is a real lever, but switching before measuring guesses at the cause.

stem: Your dashboard shows that the average latency of your Claude-backed endpoint looks fine, yet some users report waits far longer than that. How should you track latency so that this problem shows up?

choices.text: Record latency as a distribution, such as counts bucketed by latency, to expose the slow tail
choices.reason: Correct: the SRE book warns against designing around the mean and suggests request counts bucketed by latency, which separates a slow average from a very slow tail.

choices.text: Keep the average, but sample it far more often so that every slow request moves the number sooner
choices.reason: A more frequent average is still an average; the SRE book's point is that a mean can hide a tail of very slow requests.

choices.text: Measure only the fastest requests, because they show what the system can really do when it's healthy
choices.reason: That hides the problem completely; the slow tail is what users are complaining about, so the measurement has to include it.

choices.text: Stop tracking latency and track the error rate alone, since slow requests eventually become errors
choices.reason: Latency and errors are separate golden signals; a request that is slow but succeeds never shows up in an error rate.

takeaway: A good **average** can hide a slow **tail**: record latency as a distribution, not just a mean.
explanation: Latency is one of the core signals to monitor, but a mean blends a few very slow requests into many fast ones. Users reporting long waits while the average looks fine is the classic sign of a slow tail, and bucketed counts (a histogram) make it visible. Choice b is tempting because more data points sound better, but sampling an average more often still averages the tail away.

stem: Your dashboard tracks token usage and latency for every Claude call. Users report that one feature sometimes returns nothing at all, yet both charts look normal. What should you add to your per-call metrics?

choices.text: The word count of each prompt, since long prompts are the most common reason that calls fail
choices.reason: Prompt length already shows up in token usage, and it doesn't tell you how many requests failed.

choices.text: The error rate: the share of calls that fail, tracked per call as a signal of its own
choices.reason: Correct: errors, the rate of requests that fail, are one of the four golden signals, tracked alongside latency.

choices.text: A daily average of latency, so slow calls and failed calls blend into a single number
choices.reason: Averages hide problems: the SRE book warns against designing monitoring around the mean.

choices.text: Nothing new, since a call that used tokens and returned quickly must have succeeded
choices.reason: Requests can fail quickly; the SRE book notes that errors can be served fast, so speed and token use don't prove success.

takeaway: Per call, track **tokens**, **latency** and **error rate**: a cheap, fast call can still be a failed one.
explanation: Tokens and latency show cost and speed, but not whether a call worked, so error rate is the third per-call signal. The stem's clue is a failure that shows up in neither existing chart. Choice d is tempting because a call that used tokens seems to have done its job, but requests can fail quickly and still look normal on cost and latency charts.

stem: A support widget calls Claude for short answers and feels slow. The quality of its answers is already good, and now you want lower latency. Which two changes does Anthropic's latency guide recommend?

choices.text: Add more background detail to every prompt so that the model never needs to ask a follow-up
choices.reason: The guide says the fewer tokens the model has to process and generate, the faster the response, so padding every prompt works against latency.

choices.text: Choose a faster model that fits the task, such as Haiku for a speed-critical application
choices.reason: Correct: choosing the right model is one of the most direct ways to cut latency, and the guide points to Haiku for the fastest responses.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` well above the expected length so that the answers are never cut off
choices.reason: `max_tokens` is a hard limit that prevents overly long outputs; raising it doesn't make a short answer arrive any sooner.

choices.text: Keep prompts clear but concise, and ask Claude directly for shorter responses
choices.reason: Correct: minimizing input and output tokens is the guide's second strategy, by being clear but concise and asking Claude to curb its chattiness.

choices.text: Switch to the largest model at its highest effort, since stronger models finish their work sooner
choices.reason: The guide notes that model size influences latency and recommends the fastest model, at low effort, for speed-critical work.

takeaway: The latency levers: a **faster model** for the job, and **fewer tokens** in and out.
explanation: Latency depends on the model and on how many tokens are processed and generated, so the guide's first levers are the model and the prompt and output length. The stem says quality is already good, which is the guide's cue to start reducing latency. Choice e is tempting because a stronger model sounds more efficient, but larger models at higher effort are slower, not faster.

stem: A product manager wants to route the in-app chat assistant's requests through the Message Batches API to get its discount, since users ask similar questions all day. What is the problem with this plan?

choices.text: Batches can't carry multi-turn conversations, so a chat history can't be sent as a batch request
choices.reason: Almost any Messages API request can be batched, multi-turn conversations included; the blocker is the wait, not the request format.

choices.text: Batches can't be combined with prompt caching, so the repeated questions would end up costing more
choices.reason: The batch and prompt caching discounts can stack; in a batch, cache hits are provided on a best-effort basis.

choices.text: Requests in a batch share one context, so users could see parts of each other's chats in the replies
choices.reason: Each request in a batch is processed independently, with no data leakage between requests.

choices.text: Batches run asynchronously and can take up to 24 hours, so they only suit work that can wait
choices.reason: Correct: batches suit tasks that don't need immediate responses. Most finish within an hour, but a batch can take up to 24 hours.

takeaway: Batches trade **latency** for a lower bill: right for bulk work that can wait, wrong for anything a user is waiting on.
explanation: The Message Batches API halves cost by processing requests asynchronously, so its results aren't immediate. A live chat assistant has a user waiting on every request, which rules out an hour-scale or day-scale wait. Choice b is tempting because it sounds like a real limitation, but caching works inside batches and the two discounts can stack.

stem: Per-call metrics show that one step of your pipeline takes most of its time. That step only sorts each incoming message into billing, technical or other, and it runs on your largest model. Tests show a smaller, faster model sorts just as accurately. Which change fits?

choices.text: Keep the largest model and add more examples, so it sorts each message more confidently
choices.reason: More prompt tokens make a response slower, not faster: the guide says the fewer tokens the model has to process, the faster it responds.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` for that step, so the model has more room to finish each label quickly
choices.reason: `max_tokens` is a hard cap on output length. A higher cap doesn't make a one-word label arrive any sooner.

choices.text: Move every other step onto the largest model as well, so the whole pipeline runs at one speed
choices.reason: That slows every step down. The guide says to pick the model that fits each use case's needs for speed and output quality.

choices.text: Switch just that step to the smaller, faster model, since it meets the step's quality bar
choices.reason: Correct: choosing the right model is one of the most direct ways to cut latency, picking the one that fits the task's speed and quality needs.

takeaway: **Model selection** is a budget lever: when a smaller, faster model meets a step's quality bar, use it for that step.
explanation: Choosing the right model for each use case is one of the most direct ways to cut latency, and the measurements already show which step to change. The stem says the smaller model sorts just as accurately, so quality isn't at risk. Choice a is tempting because examples often help quality, but extra prompt tokens make the slow step slower.

stem: Your app caches a long, unchanging system prompt, but the usage numbers show it never reads from the cache. You find that the code adds the current time and the user's name at the very start of the system prompt on every request. What should you change?

choices.text: Cache the time and the name on their own, so the changing part is stored apart from the rest
choices.reason: A cache entry covers the whole prefix up to its breakpoint, so a value that changes at the start still changes everything after it.

choices.text: Turn caching off, because a prompt that includes any per-request detail can never be cached
choices.reason: Per-request detail is fine once it sits after the static part: the guide says to put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix.

choices.text: Move the time and the name after the unchanging instructions, so every request starts the same
choices.reason: Correct: caching reuses an identical prefix. Put static content first, and content that varies, such as timestamps, after the point where caching ends.

choices.text: Tell Claude in the prompt to ignore the time and the name, so the cache can match on the rest
choices.reason: The cache matches the prompt's exact content (a hash of the prefix), so an instruction can't make a changed prefix match.

takeaway: Caching needs a **stable prefix**: put what stays the same first, and anything that changes per request after it.
explanation: Prompt caching only reuses work when a request begins with exactly the same content as an earlier one. Putting the time and the user's name at the very start makes the prefix different on every request, so nothing after it can be read from the cache. Choice a is tempting because it isolates the changing part, but a cache entry covers everything up to its breakpoint, so a change at the start still breaks the match.

stem: Your team is deciding where to turn on prompt caching first. Which workload would benefit most from it?

choices.text: A one-off request that summarizes a single short email and is never sent again
choices.reason: Caching pays off when a later request reuses the same prefix. A one-off request has nothing to reuse.

choices.text: An agent loop where every step resends the same long instructions and tool definitions
choices.reason: Correct: caching resumes from a prefix already processed, which suits prompts with consistent elements and agentic tool use, where each step is a new API call.

choices.text: A stream of short prompts that each start with completely different text and share nothing
choices.reason: The cache only helps when requests begin with the same content. Prompts that share nothing never get a hit.

choices.text: A help bot that must give fresh answers, so its earlier replies can't be stored and reused
choices.reason: Prompt caching reuses the processing of the prompt's prefix, not Claude's answers. Every response is still generated fresh.

takeaway: Prompt caching pays off when many requests **start with the same long content**, such as an agent loop resending its instructions and tools.
explanation: Prompt caching stores the processing work for a prefix so that later requests starting with the same content can reuse it. An agent loop resends the same instructions and tool definitions on every step, so nearly every request after the first can read from the cache. Choice d is tempting because caching sounds like storing answers, but it reuses prompt processing, and responses are still generated fresh.

stem: Your product has two Claude features: a chat assistant that customers use live, and a nightly job that re-tags 50,000 old support tickets for a report read the next morning. Cost matters for both. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Stream the chat replies, and run the nightly re-tagging through the Message Batches API
choices.reason: Correct: batches suit work that doesn't need an immediate response, like the nightly job. The chat has a customer waiting, so it stays live and streamed.

choices.text: Run both through the Message Batches API, since cost matters for both and batches cost less
choices.reason: Batches run asynchronously and can take up to 24 hours. That suits the nightly job, not a customer waiting in a chat.

choices.text: Run both as live requests, since the batch discount only applies to very small jobs
choices.reason: Batches are built for large volumes of requests that don't need immediate responses, and the nightly job is exactly that.

choices.text: Batch the chat replies and stream the nightly job, so that each user sees the fastest result
choices.reason: That's reversed: the chat needs immediate responses, while nobody watches the nightly job as it runs.

takeaway: **Stream** what a person is waiting for; **batch** bulk work that can wait, at a lower cost.
explanation: Streaming and batching sit at opposite ends of the latency trade-off. The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at a lower cost, which fits a nightly job whose results are read the next morning, while the live chat has a customer waiting on every reply. Choice b is tempting because cost matters for both, but a batch can take hours to finish, which a live chat can't accept.

stem: You're reviewing proposals to cut an agent workload's spend, and you must tell the team what each one costs in return. Which two statements are accurate?

choices.text: Prompt caching: lower cost, paid for with slower responses on each cached request
choices.reason: The guide counts caching as a free win: each cached resend costs less and processes faster, without touching quality.

choices.text: Batch processing: a large discount, paid for in latency, since results can take up to a day
choices.reason: Correct: batch processing trades latency for its discount, with results arriving any time within 24 hours, so it suits work that can wait.

choices.text: Lower effort: less cost and often faster, but accuracy can drop, so check your evals
choices.reason: Correct: lower effort costs less and is often faster, but how much accuracy you lose depends on the task, so check the score on your own tasks.

choices.text: A tight `max_tokens` cap: lower cost with no effect on quality, since Claude plans to fit
choices.reason: The guide lists output caps as a tradeoff and says `max_tokens` caps a response invisibly to the model, so answers can simply be cut off.

choices.text: A smaller model: lower cost and latency, with the same accuracy on every kind of task
choices.reason: The guide lists model choice as a tradeoff that exchanges cost for intelligence, and says to compare models on cost per completed task.

takeaway: Know what each lever costs: caching is a free win, batch costs latency, and effort, caps and smaller models can cost quality.
explanation: Anthropic's cost guide splits levers into free wins, which cut spend without touching quality, and tradeoffs, which exchange cost for intelligence. Batch costs nothing in quality but pays in latency, and lower effort is a tradeoff whose accuracy cost depends on the task. Choice a is the tempting trap: caching is the rare lever that cuts cost and speeds things up at the same time.

stem: A support agent resends the same long instructions and its growing conversation on every turn. It's over budget and a little slow. One proposal turns on prompt caching; another moves the agent to a smaller model. How do the two compare?

choices.text: Both trade away quality, so pick whichever one saves more and accept the drop
choices.reason: The guide counts caching as a free win that cuts spend without touching quality. Only the model switch exchanges cost for intelligence.

choices.text: The smaller model is the free win, while caching is the one that puts quality at risk
choices.reason: It's the other way round: caching cuts spend without touching quality, and the guide lists model choice among the tradeoffs.

choices.text: Caching only cuts latency, so the smaller model is the only way to bring cost down
choices.reason: Each cached resend costs much less than the full input price and also processes faster, so caching cuts cost and latency together.

choices.text: Caching cuts cost and latency at no quality cost; a smaller model needs evals first
choices.reason: Correct: caching is a free win, to turn on before any other lever since each turn resends the conversation. A model switch is a tradeoff, so check its score on your tasks.

takeaway: Take the free wins, such as caching, first; a smaller model is a tradeoff to check with evals before you switch.
explanation: The cost guide separates free wins, which cut spend without touching quality, from tradeoffs, which exchange cost for intelligence. Caching a prefix that every turn resends is the textbook free win, and it speeds processing too. Choice c is tempting if you think of caching as a latency feature, but cached reads are also billed far below the normal input price.

diagram.caption: Free wins cut spend without touching quality; tradeoffs exchange cost for intelligence.

stem: A live writing assistant must answer while users wait, stay within a monthly budget and pass a quality bar. Your evals show Claude Haiku 5.5 misses the bar and Claude Sonnet 5.5 clears it. Every request starts with the same long block of instructions. Which plan fits all three?

choices.text: Opus 5.5 at its highest effort, since the quality bar matters more than the rest
choices.reason: Sonnet already clears the bar. A higher tier at its highest effort costs more and is slower, spending budget and time on quality you do not need.

choices.text: Sonnet 5.5, with prompt caching turned on for the shared block of instructions
choices.reason: Correct: Sonnet clears the bar, and caching is a free win: each cached resend costs less and processes faster, without touching quality.

choices.text: Haiku 5.5 with a tight `max_tokens` cap, as the fastest and cheapest option
choices.reason: Haiku already misses the quality bar, and `max_tokens` caps a response invisibly to the model, so a tight cap cuts answers off rather than improving them.

choices.text: Sonnet 5.5 through batch processing, so that the discount keeps it under budget
choices.reason: Batch trades latency for its discount, with results arriving any time within 24 hours. Users here are waiting on every answer.

takeaway: To balance all three, choose the cheapest model that clears the bar, then add free wins such as caching.
explanation: When speed, cost and quality all constrain you, no single lever wins. Evals rule out Haiku on quality, a waiting user rules out batch, and the budget argues against the top tier when Sonnet already passes. Caching the repeated instructions then cuts cost and latency together. Choice a is tempting because quality is a hard requirement, but Sonnet already meets it.

stem: You run two agent jobs on Claude Opus 5.5. Job A debugs one failure, where each step depends on the last. Job B reviews thousands of independent support transcripts, far more than one context window holds. Where does an Opus orchestrator delegating to lower-cost workers fit best?

choices.text: Both jobs, since cheaper workers lower the bill on any kind of agent task
choices.reason: Delegation saved money only in some situations. For one dependent chain, the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead in every case measured.

choices.text: Job A only, since dependent steps gain the most from a planner handing them out
choices.reason: A single dependent chain is exactly where the guide's measurements favored the orchestrator's model alone, at lower effort, over delegation.

choices.text: Job B only, since independent pieces beyond one context window suit delegation
choices.reason: Correct: the orchestrator pattern fits work that fans out across genuinely independent files, documents or cases, especially more than one context window of it.

choices.text: Neither job, since mixing models always scores lower than a single model does
choices.reason: Pairing a lower-cost model with a frontier model is a strategy the guide describes; its advice is to measure a pairing on your workload, not to rule it out.

takeaway: Delegate to lower-cost workers when work fans out into independent pieces; keep a single dependent chain on one model.
explanation: Anthropic's cost guide describes an orchestrator that plans, dispatches bulk work to lower-cost workers and synthesizes the results. In its measurements, delegation saved money on work larger than one context window, for a somewhat lower score, but not on one dependent chain, where the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead. Choice b is tempting because planning sounds useful for hard debugging, but the measurements favored a single model there.

diagram.caption: The stronger model runs the loop; lower-cost workers take the independent bulk work.

stem: Your coding agent spends most turns on routine edits, with a few hard design decisions along the way. You want those decisions to get a stronger model's judgment without paying frontier rates on every turn. Which setup fits that shape of work?

choices.text: A smaller executor runs the loop and consults a stronger model on hard calls
choices.reason: Correct: the advisor pattern fits serial work that is hard in spots. The smaller model runs the loop and escalates on demand, so most tokens bill at the lower rate.

choices.text: A frontier orchestrator splits the task across many workers running in parallel
choices.reason: The orchestrator pattern fits work that fans out across independent pieces. This is one serial task with a few hard spots.

choices.text: Every turn on the frontier model, since any setup that mixes models costs more
choices.reason: The most capable model can be too expensive at scale; multi-model strategies spend frontier intelligence on the hard tail without frontier rates for the rest.

choices.text: Models alternating turn by turn, so that each one handles half of the work
choices.reason: A fixed split ignores where the hard decisions fall. The advisor pattern brings in the stronger model on demand, when the work is hard.

takeaway: For serial work that's hard only in spots, let a smaller model run the loop and escalate hard calls to a stronger advisor.
explanation: Anthropic's cost guide describes two multi-model patterns: an executor that escalates hard decisions to an advisor, and an orchestrator that delegates bulk work. The stem's work is one serial task with a few hard spots, which is the advisor's shape. Choice b is tempting because it also mixes models, but it suits independent pieces. Note that an advisor helps only when the executor actually consults it, so measure the consult rate on your own tasks.

stem: Every request from your support bot looks like this, with a new time and question each time. Usage shows `cache_creation_input_tokens` above 0 on every request and `cache_read_input_tokens` always 0. Which change gets later requests reading the cached guide?

choices.text: Keep the breakpoint where it is; the cache lookback will walk back and find the guide by itself
choices.reason: Lookback finds entries that earlier requests **wrote**, and writes happen only at breakpoints. No request ever wrote an entry at the guide, so there is nothing to find.

choices.text: Move `cache_control` to the system block that holds the guide
choices.reason: Correct: put the breakpoint on the last block that stays identical across requests, at the end of the static prefix rather than on the varying block.

choices.text: Add `"ttl": "1h"` to the current `cache_control` so the entry lives longer
choices.reason: Lifetime isn't the problem. The time and question change, so the prefix hash at this breakpoint differs on every request, and each one pays for a fresh write.

choices.text: Move the timestamp to the start of the system prompt, so the user block changes less
choices.reason: The prefix runs `tools`, `system`, then `messages`, so a changing value at the start of `system` would change every hash after it, and the question still varies.

takeaway: Put `cache_control` at the end of the static prefix; a breakpoint on per-request content writes a new entry every time and never reads.
explanation: A breakpoint writes one cache entry: a hash of everything up to and including that block. Here it sits on the user block, whose time and question change, so every request writes a fresh entry and none reads one, which is exactly what the usage fields show. Moving it to the guide's system block caches the stable prefix. Choice a is the subtle trap: lookback only finds earlier writes, never stable content on its own.

stem: This nightly job submits a Message Batch, then writes each summary back once processing has ended. Some products get another product's summary, and the job sometimes crashes partway through the results. Which two changes fix the results loop?

snippet.code:
requests = [
    Request(
        custom_id=f"product-{p.id}",
        params=MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming(
            model="claude-haiku-5-5",
            max_tokens=512,
            messages=[{"role": "user",
                       "content": p.prompt}],
        ),
    )
    for p in products
]
batch = client.messages.batches.create(
    requests=requests)
# ...later, once processing has ended:
results = client.messages.batches.results(batch.id)
for p, r in zip(products, results):
    msg = r.result.message
    p.summary = msg.content[0].text

choices.text: Look up each product by `r.custom_id` instead of pairing results with `products` by position
choices.reason: Correct: results can come back in any order, not necessarily the order of the requests, so match each result to its request with `custom_id`.

choices.text: Check `r.result.type` and read `message` only when it is `"succeeded"`; handle `errored` and `expired` results separately
choices.reason: Correct: only a `succeeded` result includes the message. For `errored` and `expired` requests no message was created, so branch on the type first.

choices.text: Sort `products` by ID before building the batch, so the results come back in the same order
choices.reason: Batch results can be returned in any order, whatever order the requests were in. Always use the `custom_id` field to match them.

choices.text: Use each product's list position, such as `"0"` and `"1"`, as its `custom_id` so results line up with the list
choices.reason: The IDs aren't the problem; ignoring them is. Results arrive in any order, so the loop has to look each one up by its `custom_id`.

choices.text: Read results while the batch is still in progress, so fewer of them go missing
choices.reason: You retrieve results once processing has ended for all requests. Reading earlier fixes neither the ordering nor the failed requests.

takeaway: Join batch results to inputs by `custom_id`, and check `result.type` before reading a message.
explanation: Two bugs hide in the last four lines. `zip` assumes results arrive in request order, but they can come back in any order, so the job must look each one up by the `custom_id` it already set. And it reads `.message` from every result, though only `succeeded` results include one. Choice c is tempting, but ordering the requests doesn't order the results.

stem: Your batch job resubmits failures with the code below. A few requests come back `errored` in every new batch, night after night. What should the job do differently?

choices.text: Resubmit the failures in smaller batches, since large batches are more likely to hit errors
choices.reason: Each request in a batch is processed independently, so batch size isn't why the same requests fail every time.

choices.text: Stop retrying errored requests: each attempt is billed, so the repeats cost more than they recover
choices.reason: Errored requests aren't billed. The real issue is that some of them can never succeed as written.

choices.text: Check `outcome.error.error.type`: fix `invalid_request_error` bodies before resending, and resubmit the rest as they are
choices.reason: Correct: an invalid request's body must be fixed before you send it again, while other errors, such as server errors, can be retried directly.

choices.text: Send the failing requests one at a time through the synchronous Messages API instead
choices.reason: An invalid request body fails wherever you send it; the batch guide says it must be fixed before re-sending. Switching APIs also gives up the batch discount.

takeaway: Split `errored` batch results by error type: fix invalid requests, and retry server errors as they are.
explanation: An `errored` result can mean an invalid request or an internal server error. This loop resubmits every errored request unchanged, so one with an invalid body fails the same way in every batch. Reading the error type separates the requests to fix from the ones to retry directly. Choice b is tempting as cost control, but errored requests aren't billed; the waste is resending requests that can't succeed.

stem: Your platform picks each task's model with this function. Triage runs about 50,000 times a day and only labels a ticket with one of six queues. Audits run a few times a week as multihour autonomous refactors. Bills are high and the audits are weak. Which change fits Anthropic's model-selection guide?

choices.text: Return `claude-opus-5-5` for both kinds, since the guide says most workloads start with Opus 5.5
choices.reason: High-volume, straightforward, cost-sensitive tasks like triage are the cases the guide gives for starting with Haiku 5.5, and the bill is already the problem.

choices.text: Swap the return values: `claude-haiku-5-5` for triage and `claude-opus-5-5` for the audits
choices.reason: Correct: the guide matches high-volume, cost-sensitive work to Claude Haiku 5.5 and multihour autonomous coding agents to Claude Opus 5.5.

choices.text: Return `claude-haiku-5-5` for both kinds, since starting efficiency-first keeps every task cheapest
choices.reason: Efficiency-first means upgrading where there's a capability gap. The guide lists multihour autonomous coding agents under Opus 5.5, and the audits are already weak.

choices.text: Route triage to `claude-fable-5-1`, since a wrong queue label is the costliest mistake here
choices.reason: Fable 5.1 is for the highest capability, such as agent sessions that run for hours; labelling tickets at volume is the low-latency, low-price case for Haiku 5.5.

takeaway: Route by the task: Haiku for high-volume, simple work; Opus for long, complex agentic work.
explanation: The function has its two branches backwards. Anthropic's guide points high-volume, cost-sensitive work like ticket triage to Claude Haiku 5.5 and multihour autonomous coding to Claude Opus 5.5, so swapping the return values cuts the bill and strengthens the audits. Choice a is tempting because the guide says most workloads start with Opus 5.5, but triage at this volume is the case it gives for Haiku.

stem: Two reviewers ran the same evaluation prompt on the same transcript, with the same model and settings, and got differently worded verdicts that reach the same conclusion. One files a bug. What is the most accurate response?

choices.text: A real bug: with identical request bodies the API returns identical text, so something must have altered one request
choices.reason: The glossary says the opposite: "identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls", so differing wording needs no altered request to explain it.

choices.text: Not a bug: identical inputs can produce different outputs across calls, so compare the verdicts, not the wording
choices.reason: Correct: the glossary notes that users "may encounter non-determinism in APIs" and that even at temperature 0 "identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls".

choices.text: Expected only because one reviewer streamed the reply; non-streamed requests return the same text every time
choices.reason: The glossary ties the variation to generation itself, across API calls as such; it makes no exception for non-streamed requests.

choices.text: Expected only on smaller models; the most capable tier returns identical text for identical inputs
choices.reason: The non-determinism note is about the API in general, not a model tier, and the glossary says it applies on Anthropic's own service and through third-party cloud providers alike.

takeaway: Identical inputs can yield different outputs across calls; judge replies on substance, not on exact text.
explanation: The principle is non-determinism: the glossary states that identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls, even with temperature at 0, so two runs of the same eval prompt can differ in wording with nothing wrong. The deciding detail is that the verdicts agree while only the wording differs. Option c is the tempting trap: streaming changes how a reply is delivered, not the generation that produces the variation.

stem: A teammate says: "If we want Claude to reason more carefully on this task, we have to switch to a different model." Which statement best separates model choice from reasoning depth?

choices.text: They are one lever: choosing Opus switches thinking on and choosing Haiku switches it off, so the model you pick decides the reasoning
choices.reason: The per-model table shows Claude Haiku 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 running adaptive thinking too; which family member you pick doesn't decide whether thinking happens.

choices.text: Reasoning depth is fixed per account by Anthropic, so changing the model is the only way to get deeper reasoning
choices.reason: `thinking` and `output_config.effort` are request parameters; nothing about reasoning depth is set per account.

choices.text: Model choice picks the family member; `thinking` and `effort` are per-request settings for whether and how deeply it reasons
choices.reason: Correct: "The `thinking` parameter controls whether Claude thinks ... the `effort` parameter controls how much work Claude puts into the whole response", and both are sent on each request.

choices.text: Thinking is a separate reasoning model you call instead of the chat model, so it is a model switch after all
choices.reason: Thinking is content the same model produces before its answer: "That up-front thinking arrives in `thinking` content blocks ahead of the response." No second model is involved.

takeaway: Pick the model for capability and price; set `thinking` and `effort` per request for reasoning depth.
explanation: Model choice and reasoning depth are two separate, composable levers: which model serves the request, and whether and how deeply it thinks, controlled per request with `thinking` and `effort`. The teammate's claim collapses them into one. Option a is the trap: it assumes thinking belongs to a tier, but the current Haiku and Sonnet models run adaptive thinking as well, so a model switch is not how you get more reasoning.

stem: A design review asks what happens to a chat assistant whose stored history is appended to on every turn and never trimmed, as weeks of conversation accumulate. Which prediction is accurate?

choices.text: The API silently drops the oldest turns so the newest message always fits, so nothing in the app needs to change as history grows
choices.reason: In API requests "previous turns are preserved completely"; rolling first-in, first-out trimming is something chat interfaces do, not the API.

choices.text: The window expands on demand to hold the extra turns; the only effect is a higher bill for the additional tokens
choices.reason: The context window is a fixed per-model limit. Tokens beyond it are rejected or end generation; they aren't billed as overflow.

choices.text: Oversized input gets a 400 before generation; if generation hits the limit, output stops with `model_context_window_exceeded`
choices.reason: Correct: "If the input alone already exceeds the model's context window, the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error", and generation that reaches the limit "stops with stop_reason: model_context_window_exceeded".

choices.text: Nothing changes until `max_tokens` is reached, because the window limits the output Claude writes, not the input
choices.reason: The window "holds the conversation history plus the new output"; every message, tool result and tool definition in the request counts toward it.

takeaway: The window is a fixed budget for input plus output; trimming or compacting history is the application's job.
explanation: A context window is a fixed budget that holds the whole history plus the new output, so an untrimmed history eventually fills it. Two behaviours follow: input already over the limit fails with a 400 before generation, and generation that reaches the limit stops with `model_context_window_exceeded` and truncated output. Managing history is the app's job. Option a is the trap: FIFO trimming is a chat-interface behaviour, not something the API does for you.

stem: A nightly job on Claude Haiku 5.5 sorts the day's support emails, tens of thousands of them, into eight fixed categories. Latency and cost per email matter, and each decision is a quick lookup rather than a multi-step problem. How should thinking be set?

choices.text: Raise `effort` to `max`, because at this volume every misfiled email is expensive and deeper reasoning prevents it
choices.reason: `max` makes Claude think "the most readily and at the greatest depth"; thinking tokens are billed as output on every one of tens of thousands of requests, for a task that doesn't need reasoning.

choices.text: Keep the default effort and tell it in the system prompt to answer directly without deliberating on each email
choices.reason: The page says to lower effort before prompt-based steering, and that in Anthropic's testing telling Claude Haiku 5.5 to answer directly "didn't stop it from thinking".

choices.text: Move the job to Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort, since a stronger model reasons more reliably
choices.reason: This raises cost without touching the control that matters: effort decides how readily Claude thinks, and the task needs less thinking, not a bigger model.

choices.text: Lower `effort` to `low` so simple lookups skip thinking; disable thinking outright if evals still hold
choices.reason: Correct: at `low`, "Claude minimizes thinking. Skips thinking for simple tasks where speed matters most", and lowering effort is the recommended first lever for less thinking.

takeaway: Mechanical, lookup-style work gets the lowest effort; reach for prompt steering only after effort is set.
explanation: Match reasoning depth to the task before tuning anything else: fixed-category classification is a lookup, so the lowest effort (which skips thinking on simple tasks) is right, and thinking can be disabled where the model allows it. The deciding details are "quick lookup" and "cost per email". Option b is the trap: on Haiku 5.5 a prompt instruction to answer directly did not reliably reduce thinking in Anthropic's testing; effort is the calibrated control.

stem: You're writing the thinking policy for three workloads: a record-format conversion job, a tool-using agent, and a data-pipeline redesign planner whose steps depend on each other. Which two decisions are right?

choices.text: Pipeline redesign planner: keep thinking on and raise `effort` if its plans come out shallow
choices.reason: Correct: thinking helps "complex tasks like math, coding, analysis, and long-running agentic work", and when Claude is "thinking too rarely or too shallowly: raise effort".

choices.text: Format conversion job: raise `effort` to `max`, because volume makes any mistake costly
choices.reason: For lower cost or latency the page says to "lower effort first"; thinking is billed as output tokens, so maximum effort on a mechanical job multiplies cost for no reasoning benefit.

choices.text: Tool-using agent: echo each assistant turn back unchanged, thinking blocks included, when returning tool results
choices.reason: Correct: "Required: within a tool-use turn, pass thinking blocks back", complete and unmodified; "Modified thinking blocks are rejected with a 400 error."

choices.text: Tool-using agent: strip thinking blocks before returning tool results to save context
choices.reason: Inside a tool-use turn the blocks are required, and "You don't need to prune old thinking yourself": pass everything back and the API filters prior-turn blocks per model.

choices.text: Pipeline redesign planner: set `output_config.effort` to `adaptive` so Claude chooses its own depth on every planning step
choices.reason: "Don't pass `adaptive` as an `effort` value: `adaptive` is a thinking mode, not an effort level." Effort levels are `low` through `max`.

takeaway: Match effort to the task's reasoning load, and never edit or drop thinking blocks inside a tool-use turn.
explanation: Two rules from the thinking docs: effort is the dial for reasoning depth (raise it for dependent multi-step planning, lower it for mechanical work), and within a tool-use turn the thinking blocks must go back exactly as received. Option d is the trap: stripping blocks to save context breaks the turn, and the API already prunes prior-turn thinking where the model does so. Option e misuses `adaptive`, which is a thinking mode, not an effort level.

stem: You're deciding how each image reaches the API in an equipment-inspection app. The same equipment schematic accompanies every inspection; a technician occasionally attaches a one-off photo of a fault. Which two pairings fit?

choices.text: Equipment schematic: upload it once to the Files API and reference its `file_id` in each request
choices.reason: Correct: "For images you'll use repeatedly ... upload the image once, then reference the returned `file_id` in subsequent messages instead of resending base64 data."

choices.text: One-off fault photo: embed it as a base64 `image` block in that single request
choices.reason: Correct: a base64-encoded image embedded in the request body is one of the three documented sources, and the Files API is positioned for images you'll use repeatedly.

choices.text: Equipment schematic: send base64 on every request, because the Files API only accepts PDFs
choices.reason: The page shows an `image` block whose `source` is `{"type": "file", "file_id": ...}`; images are a supported Files API type.

choices.text: One-off photo: route it through the Files API first, since base64 image sources are deprecated
choices.reason: Base64 is a current source type, and on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud it is the only one available; nothing marks it deprecated.

choices.text: Multi-turn review of one schematic: re-send it as base64 on every turn so Claude doesn't forget what it looks like
choices.reason: "Claude has access to every image from earlier turns", and base64 in history means "the full image bytes are included in the payload on every turn", growing request size and latency.

takeaway: Upload what repeats and reference it by `file_id`; inline base64 is fine for an image you send once.
explanation: The rule is reuse: an image that goes into many requests should be uploaded once and referenced by `file_id`, which keeps every payload small; an image sent once can simply be embedded as base64. Option e is the trap: Claude already sees earlier turns' images, so re-sending base64 each turn only bloats the request. Options c and d both misstate what the Files API and base64 support.

stem: Your cost review lists five Claude workloads. Which two should move to the Message Batches API?

choices.text: Re-scoring 30,000 archived product reviews for sentiment overnight
choices.reason: Correct: bulk work that needs no immediate result. The page lists summaries and insights for large datasets among batch uses, and all usage is charged at 50% of standard prices.

choices.text: The checkout page's address-correction suggestion the shopper is waiting on
choices.reason: Someone is waiting. Batches are for tasks that "do not require immediate responses"; results arrive when processing ends, up to 24 hours later.

choices.text: A regression eval over the saved test set before each release
choices.reason: Correct: the page lists "Large-scale evaluations: Process thousands of test cases efficiently" as a typical batch use.

choices.text: Live translation of each message in a support chat
choices.reason: A live reply needs an immediate response, which the asynchronous batch path doesn't provide.

choices.text: A nightly report whose single request must be guaranteed to finish within one minute
choices.reason: Batches offer no completion-time guarantee: most finish within 1 hour, results are available by 24 hours at the latest, and requests can expire.

takeaway: Batch what nobody waits on: bulk jobs and eval runs; keep user-facing turns synchronous.
explanation: The deciding question is whether anyone waits on the result. Overnight review scoring and a pre-release eval run are bulk, offline work, which the Batches API handles asynchronously at half price. The shopper's address check and each live translation have a person waiting, so they stay synchronous. Option e is the trap: it is offline, but a hard one-minute deadline is something a batch cannot promise.

stem: A logistics platform labels every package-scan note (damaged, delayed, delivered) in real time, tens of millions a day. Your eval on real notes shows Claude Haiku 5.5 meets the accuracy bar. Which choice fits, and what decides it?

choices.text: Claude Opus 5.5, because the most capable model is the safest default for any production workload
choices.reason: Opus is the suggested start when you're unsure, but the eval already answers the question; paying its higher per-token price for tens of millions of notes buys nothing the bar requires.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5, because a middle tier hedges against the eval being wrong on rare note types
choices.reason: An eval on real notes is the evidence; hedging with a slower, pricier tier doesn't address a gap the eval didn't find.

choices.text: Claude Fable 5.1, because volume this high needs the strongest reasoning available
choices.reason: Fable is for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short; a simple label is neither.

choices.text: Claude Haiku 5.5, because the eval already clears the bar and price at this volume is what is left to decide
choices.reason: Correct: Haiku 5.5 is for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction and routing; once the eval confirms quality, cost at volume decides.

takeaway: High volume plus an eval that passes on the smallest tier means **Haiku**: the bar is met, so cost at volume is the deciding constraint.
explanation: Model choice pairs a tier with the constraint that decides it. The eval removes quality as the open question, leaving volume, so the fastest and cheapest tier wins. Option a is tempting because Opus is the suggested start for most workloads when unsure, but this team isn't unsure: it has an eval.

stem: An agent analyzes a contract in stages that each build on the last; an error in an early stage invalidates everything after it. Your eval shows Claude Sonnet 5.5 fails on the most intricate contracts. Which choice fits, and what decides it?

choices.text: Claude Opus 5.5, because quality on hard reasoning decides when a wrong step is costly
choices.reason: Correct: start capability-first when accuracy outweighs cost, as in complex reasoning and high-autonomy agentic work; Opus is the strongest starting point short of Fable.

choices.text: Claude Haiku 5.5, because the stages are small and speed keeps the analysis short
choices.reason: Efficiency-first suits high-volume, straightforward tasks and tight latency budgets; nobody is waiting on this analysis, and the intricate contracts are the risk.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5 with retries, because rerunning a failed stage is cheaper than a bigger model
choices.reason: The eval shows Sonnet fails the most intricate contracts; retrying the same model doesn't close a capability gap, and each early error here voids the stages after it.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5, because the balance of speed and intelligence suits every agentic job
choices.reason: Sonnet is the speed-and-capability balance for everyday work, but the eval says this job's hardest cases exceed it, which is the specific capability gap that justifies upgrading.

takeaway: When an error is expensive and the eval shows the cheaper tier missing hard cases, the deciding constraint is **quality**: go up a tier.
explanation: The two facts that decide this are the cost of an early error and the eval result. Together they make quality on hard reasoning the constraint, which is the capability-first case. Option c is tempting because retries are cheap, but retries don't close a capability gap the eval has already shown, and here each miss invalidates everything after it.

stem: An internal IT helpdesk assistant gets mostly simple requests (password resets, where-is-this-setting) and a few long troubleshooting threads that need real synthesis. Finance wants the common path cheap. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Claude Opus 5.5 for every request, because the hard troubleshooting threads set the quality bar for the entire service
choices.reason: Running the most capable model on the common, simple path pays frontier prices for work a smaller model handles; routing keeps that spend for the hard cases.
