choices.text: Claude Haiku 5.5 for everything, because most requests are simple and the hard ones can be retried
choices.reason: Routing sends hard or unusual questions to a more capable model precisely because the small one handles them poorly; retrying doesn't add capability.

choices.text: A fast default with an override to Claude Opus 5.5 when a signal marks the request complex
choices.reason: Correct: routing classifies an input and directs it to the right follow-up, such as easy questions to a smaller, cost-efficient model and hard ones to a more capable model; it fits when categories are distinct.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5 for everything, because one middle tier avoids building and maintaining a classifier
choices.reason: One tier for mixed traffic overpays simple requests or underserves the hard threads; routing works well when there are distinct categories better handled separately.

takeaway: Mixed traffic calls for **routing**: a cheap default plus an override to a capable model when a task signal says the request is hard.
explanation: The stem gives two distinct categories with different needs and a cost target on the common path, which is the routing pattern's home ground. Option d is tempting as a compromise, but a single tier can't be cheap for the simple majority and strong for the few hard threads at once.

diagram.caption: Most requests take the cheap path; a signal sends the hard ones up a tier.

stem: You're matching workloads to designs under a tight budget. Which two pairings fit?

choices.text: Live chat where the user watches the reply → send it through the Batch API to get the discount
choices.reason: The Batch API is for requests no one is waiting on, with results arriving any time within 24 hours; the interactive path stays synchronous.

choices.text: Weekly due-diligence scan of 400 independent company filings → a frontier orchestrator delegating the bulk reading to lower-cost workers
choices.reason: Correct: the orchestrator strategy fits work that fans out across genuinely independent files, documents or cases, with the frontier model planning and synthesizing.

choices.text: One short policy question answered from a stable handbook → a lead agent fanning out to parallel subagents for accuracy
choices.reason: Work that fits in a single context without a long cost tail came out ahead on a single model; fan-out adds coordination and tokens for nothing.

choices.text: Nightly re-tagging of old tickets nobody reads until morning → the Batch API with prompt caching on the shared instructions
choices.reason: Correct: route work no one is waiting on through the Batch API, which takes 50% off every token, and turn on prompt caching for the repeated prefix.

choices.text: A schema migration whose steps each depend on the last → split it across parallel workers to finish sooner
choices.reason: When the work is one dependent chain, a single model at lower effort came out ahead in every case measured; parallel workers can't run steps that wait on each other.

takeaway: Fan out only when the work splits into independent parts; batch only when nobody is waiting; everything else is a single agent.
explanation: Each pairing turns on one question: does the work split (orchestrator), and is anyone waiting (batch)? Pairing b splits across independent filings and d is unattended, so both fit. Options a and e are tempting because batches are cheap and parallelism is fast, but a user is waiting in a, and e's steps depend on one another.

stem: An HR assistant answers single-fact questions (holiday allowance, expense limits) from a 40-page handbook that changes once a year. A proposal replaces it with a lead agent on Claude Opus 5.5 that fans out to four research subagents per question. What should the team do?

choices.text: Adopt it: several agents reading the same handbook in parallel raise accuracy on every question and cut latency
choices.reason: Delegation saved money only for routine work with a long cost tail or work larger than one context window; a 40-page handbook is neither.

choices.text: Keep one model answering from the handbook; fan-out pays off when work splits across independent documents
choices.reason: Correct: when the work fits in a single context without a long cost tail, the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead in every case measured.

choices.text: Adopt it, but run the four subagents on Claude Haiku 5.5 so the whole fan-out costs about the same as a single call
choices.reason: Cheaper workers don't remove the orchestrator's planning, dispatch and synthesis; a pairing has to beat a single model's whole curve of score against spend, and here it can't.

choices.text: Keep one agent but move it to Claude Fable 5.1, because the questions deserve the most capable model
choices.reason: Fable is for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short; a single-fact lookup isn't that.

takeaway: A single-fact lookup over a stable corpus is one agent, one model, fetch once; **orchestration** is for work that genuinely fans out.
explanation: The deciding detail is that each question is one fact from a corpus that fits in a single context. Multi-model orchestration earns its extra tokens only when work splits across independent documents or exceeds a context window. Option c is tempting because cheap workers sound free, but the pairing still has to beat a single model's cost-versus-score curve, and this workload gives it nothing to win on.
